          "msg_id": "M80",
          "speaker_id": 204917,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Time to plan how we roll this out.\nI have drafted a short toolbox talk script for the new sorting, cleaning and reporting routines, which will become A7 and supports T8.\nIt covers:\n- key changes in A1, A2, A3 and A4.\n- the incident steps from A5.\n- a quick check of understanding.\nWe also need to confirm PPE and signage needs for T10 and agree on a go-live date for the pilot and then full line.\nPlease review the script and share any tweaks or missing points.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A7",
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A4",
            "A5",
            "T8",
            "T10",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            31940,
            307206,
            41356,
            468833,
            489662
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M81",
          "speaker_id": 41356,
          "reply_to": "M80",
          "text": "The script in A7 reads well.\nI suggest we keep it to 15 minutes max and use simple questions like: 'Where do batteries go now?' and 'What are the three steps if you see a spill or near miss?'.\nFor PPE and signage under T10, we should list:\n- gloves, safety glasses, high-vis, safety shoes as standard.\n- extra face shields when draining liquids.\n- clear signs for the pedestrian lane, no-parking zone, and hazardous cage rules.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A7",
            "A5",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            204917
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M82",
          "speaker_id": 468833,
          "reply_to": "M80",
          "text": "On the training content, we should also include a quick demo of how to use A2 and where to find A3 and A5 on the wall.\nFor new staff, I can later turn this into a short guideline for on-the-job coaching as part of T11.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A5",
            "A7",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            204917
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M83",
          "speaker_id": 31940,
          "reply_to": "M80",
          "text": "The script is easy to follow.\nI like the idea of asking simple questions.\nFor PPE, can we make it clear that face shields are only needed when draining or handling liquids, not all the time?\nOtherwise people might avoid using them.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A7",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            204917
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M84",
          "speaker_id": 489662,
          "reply_to": "M80",
          "text": "For signage, it would help to have:\n- a simple map of the pilot area from A6 with arrows for the forklift path and the pedestrian lane.\n- icons showing where to find A1, A2, A3, A4 and A5 on the wall.\nWe can mention that in the toolbox talk so people know where to look.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A4",
            "A5",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            204917,
            41356
          ]
        },

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:

2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:

   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of LOW  => candidate LOW

3. Attention:
   * If there are strong signals of HIGH and LOW at the same time for the same attribute, choose MID (conservative rule).
   * In the corporate context, everyone needs to deliver and demonstrate work; be careful to infer HIGH for something standard that should be MID.
   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:
   * If there are no messages from the participant, use MID for all three attributes and use evidence from a message where they were mentioned.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:
   * Messages where speaker_id == the participant’s _id.
   * If the participant speaks little, you can also use messages that mention them (mentions contains _id) as contextual evidence.
2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of HIGH => candidate HIGH
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of LOW  => candidate LOW

3. Attention:
   * If there are strong signals of HIGH and LOW at the same time for the same attribute, choose MID (conservative rule).
   * In the corporate context, everyone needs to deliver and demonstrate work; be careful to infer HIGH for something standard that should be MID.
   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:
   * If there are no messages from the participant, use MID for all three attributes and use evidence from a message where they were mentioned.

* For each participant, return 2 to 5 items in evidence.

  * msg_id must exist in the channel
  * justification: one sentence justifying the label.

* Do not invent msg_id.
* Do not include “LOW/MID/HIGH” in the snippet.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

          "text": "I have pulled together preliminary findings from T6 on the top 3 recurring mechanical faults on the main packaging line.\nSummary in A4 draft:\n1) Infeed conveyor jams leading to product pile-ups and waste.\n2) Film tracking issues causing misaligned seals and rework.\n3) Sealing jaw temperature instability leading to open or crushed packs.\nFor each, A4 lists suspected root causes, evidence from logs and operator feedback, and some candidate corrective actions.           "artifact_refs": [
            "T6",
            "A4",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [

            533175,

          "speaker_id": 386277,
          "reply_to": "M44",
          "text": "The three faults you listed match what I have seen.\nOn infeed jams, I noticed that they often happen when product spacing from the upstream process is inconsistent.           "text": "From the operator side, the list in A4 feels accurate.\nFilm tracking and sealing issues are the ones that create the most visible waste and rework on my shifts.\nFor infeed jams, I agree with 386277 that upstream spacing is a big factor.           "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 52126,
          "reply_to": "M37",
          "text": "From discussions with partners, a fixed revenue share for MVP is simpler and more acceptable, as long as it is within the typical range for eco-tourism platforms.\n\nGiven the community focus and the need to keep partners motivated, I would lean toward a partner-friendly share initially, then revisit once we have data.\n\nWe should also consider whether we want to include any small community contribution per booking in the pricing, which would need to be reflected in A2 and clearly communicated in the bundles from T2.",

          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 185576,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "Looking at A2 and the constraints, I would propose the following pricing approach for MVP:\n\n- Use a fixed partner revenue share percentage across all MVP bundles, within a range that is competitive with other platforms\n- Add a small, clearly labelled community contribution per booking, which we pass through fully to local initiatives\n- Set our margin target per booking at a modest level initially, prioritising volume and partner relationships over short-term profit\n\nWe can then model three scenarios in T5 using this structure and track the impact via the risk register in T12.",

            "A2",

          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "I support that structure. It is simple enough for MVP and aligns with the eco and community positioning.\n\nOn the customer side, we should ensure the community contribution is visible but not confusing. WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

          "msg_id": "M48",
          "speaker_id": 371640,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I want to clarify how the new changeover and rotation routines will show up in time records for project_pack_ref: Standardise Assembly Line Changeover and Ergonomic Routines.\nFor T7 and T12 we need clear rules in A7 so that:\n- Changeover time is coded consistently across shifts.\n- Rotation time does not create confusion with breaks or downtime.\nAlso, for T8 we have the weekly summary template in A6, which needs inputs from the line.\nCan you share how you currently record changeover time on Line 3 late shift, and whether you see any issues if we start coding it as a separate activity?",

          "reply_to": "M48",
          "text": "Right now on Line 3 late shift we just see changeover as part of normal working time. We do not press any special code on the terminal, we just stop the line and then start again.\nIf we add a separate code, we will need a simple rule on when to start and stop it, otherwise people will forget.",

          "speaker_id": 81330,

          "speaker_id": 371640,
          "reply_to": "M49",
          "text": "Thanks, that helps.\nMy proposal for A7 under T7 is:\n- Use one code for changeover time, started when the supervisor calls the change and the line stops, and ended when the first good part of the new product is confirmed.\n- Rotation between stations during normal running stays under normal working time, no extra code.\nThis keeps it simple and matches how we measure changeover in A6 for T8.\nAny concerns with that start and end rule?",

          "speaker_id": 10272,

          "text": "Thanks for the inputs.\nFrom what I hear so far, possible adjustments:\n- In A1, add a small note to double check the floor for loose parts right after clearing the line, to reduce the near miss risk.\n- In A2, add a simple tick box sheet or space to sign off.\n- In A3, maybe add a small reminder on the poster or at the board about the rotation move times.\nAny other changes you think we should make now, or should we keep the rest as is for another week?",

          "speaker_id": 297089,

          "text": "Moving on to the SOP and logging.\n\nI have drafted:\n- A health risk assessment and escalation SOP, captured in A5 and linked to T3\n- A central health monitoring log template A4 with a basic filing workflow under T5.\n\nThe SOP A5 covers:\n- Who is responsible for initial observation, escalation, and documentation\n- When to escalate based on the indicators in A2\n- How to record actions in A3 and transfer them into A4.\n\nThe log A4 is a simple table that can be printed and filed daily.\n\nI need your input on:\n- Whether the escalation steps and responsibilities are realistic on the floor\n- Whether the log format and storage routine fit with current correctional procedures and admin capacity.\n\nOnce we refine these, we also need to document alignment with existing rules in A8 under T11.",

          "text": "On the escalation thresholds in A5, I have aligned them with the indicators in A2:\n- Any serious breathing problem, chest pain, or loss of consciousness triggers immediate medical contact and emergency response.\n- Clear self-harm intent or attempt triggers immediate escalation to supervisor and medical.\n- Moderate concerns (for example, mild confusion, visible but not severe injury) trigger same-day medical review.\n\nThe SOP text makes it clear that emergency response always comes before paperwork.\n\nIf you see any conflict with current correctional procedures, we should adjust the wording before we finalise A5 and A8.",

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have put together a first draft of the daily vehicle inspection checklist for T1, based on what we already do plus some gaps we saw in the last month.\nStructure in A1 draft:\n- Exterior: body damage, mirrors, lights, indicators, licence plates.\n- Tyres: pressure visual check, tread, obvious cuts.\n- Fluids: oil level, coolant level, windscreen wash.\n- Interior: horn, seatbelts, dashboard warning lights, cleanliness.\n- Safety equipment: fire extinguisher, first aid kit, spill kit, reversing alarm.\nSome of the deeper checks we currently do daily might be better as weekly in T2, like detailed brake inspection and full hydraulic hose check.\nCan you review and say what is missing or too heavy for a daily routine?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "T1",
            "T2"

          "reply_to": "M17",
          "text": "Thanks for structuring it clearly.\nFrom my side, the sections look right. For daily, I would keep anything that can be checked quickly without tools and that affects safety before leaving the yard.\nI agree that detailed brake checks and full hydraulic inspections belong in the weekly deep-check in T2, not daily. For daily, maybe we just keep a simple leak and noise check when moving the vehicle.\nOne thing I would add to A1 is a quick check that the maintenance schedule status on the board in A3 matches the sticker in the cab, so we catch any mismatch early.",

          "text": "The structure makes sense to me.           "text": "I like that tyres and lights are clearly listed.           "text": "Good question on fluids.           "text": "I would keep reversing camera and alarm in the daily checklist. It is a quick test and very important for safety in the yard.\nFor weekly, we can add cleaning of the camera housing and checking the wiring if there were any issues reported.",

          "speaker_id": 203126,

          "text": "Agree with 156061. Reversing camera and alarm should stay in daily. The more we catch before moving the vehicle, the better.\nSo to summarise the split:\nDaily (A1): quick visual checks of exterior, tyres, leaks, dashboard warnings, reversing aids, safety equipment, cab condition, and a quick match against the schedule board in A3.\nWeekly (T2): detailed brakes, hydraulics, full fluid levels, detailed tyres and wheels including torque, deeper camera and wiring checks.\nIf everyone is ok with that, we can say the structure of the daily checklist is approved and these items move to weekly.",

          "text": "Starting a thread on hazardous substances and workshop standards.\nI drafted some initial ideas for the handling and storage guide in A2 for T3 and for the cleaning and tool storage standard in A6 for T9.\nKey points for chemicals and oils:\n- All containers labelled with product name and hazard pictograms.\n- Separate shelves for oils, cleaners, and fuels, with spill trays.\n- PPE list by product type, based on safety data sheets.\n- Simple spill response steps with where to find absorbent material.\nFor workshop organisation:\n- Marked zones for tools, waste, and chemicals.\n- End-of-shift checklist for sweeping, putting tools back, and emptying waste bins.\nPlease comment on what is practical for your shift and what we might be missing.",

          "speaker_id": 108987,
          "reply_to": "M32",
          "text": "For early shift, the main issue I see is open containers of degreaser and oil left on benches.\nCould we add a rule in A2 that all liquids must be stored with lids on when not in use, and that we do not use unlabelled bottles at all?\nOn cleaning, the end-of-shift checklist in A6 sounds good, but we need to keep it short so people actually do it. Maybe three or four clear steps only.",

          "text": "I agree on the labels. Sometimes we pour cleaner into old drink bottles, which is not safe.\nMaybe we should say in T3 that only approved containers from the store can be used, and if a label is damaged, we replace it before using the product.\nFor tool zones in T9, could we mark the floor with colours so it is obvious where tools and waste go? That might help new staff.",

          "text": "On late shift we often handle used oil and coolant when draining vehicles.\nI suggest A2 includes:\n- Separate labelled drums for used oil and used coolant.\n- Clear rule that we never mix different wastes in the same drum.\n- Simple instruction on what to do if a drum is nearly full, so we do not overfill.\nFor A6, I like the idea of an end-of-shift checklist. Maybe we can also add a quick check that spill kits are complete and in place.",

          "text": "One thing I see a lot is rags soaked in solvent left on benches.\nCould we define in T9 that there is a metal bin with lid just for oily and solvent rags, and that it is emptied into the correct waste container at least once per shift?\nAlso, for PPE in A2, maybe we can have a simple table on the wall: for each product, which gloves, goggles, and mask to use. That would make it easier to follow.",

          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "These are all good additions.\nOn the rules side, I propose we lock in the following for A2:\n- Only labelled, approved containers from the store, no drink bottles.\n- Lids on when not in use.\n- Separate storage and waste drums for each type of oil and coolant, clearly labelled.\n- PPE table on the wall by product.\n- Simple spill response: stop, contain, clean, report, with location of spill kits.\nIf we agree, we can say the handling and storage rules are approved and send A2 to the health and safety officer for sign-off as required in T3.",

          "text": "I am ok with those rules.           "text": "Yesterday we had a small incident: a driver almost moved truck 14 while a hose was still connected. He stopped in time, so no damage, but it was close.\nI was not sure how to log this properly. For T5 we have the idea of an incident and near-miss log in A4, but I do not know exactly which fields we want or how we flag the vehicle as not safe to leave the yard.\nCan we agree what information we record in A4 and how we mark a 'do not use' vehicle for T11?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126,
            38857,
            109283,
            156061
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M48",
          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": "M47",
          "text": "Thanks for raising it, that is exactly the kind of near-miss we want to capture.\nFor A4, I suggest we keep the fields simple:\n- Date and time.\n- Vehicle ID.\n- Location (yard, workshop bay, on route).\n- Type (incident or near-miss).\n- Short description of what happened.\n- Immediate action taken.\n- Follow-up action needed and by when.\nFor 'do not use' in T11, we need both a physical tag on the vehicle and a note on the schedule board in A3 so no one misses it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T11",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M49",
          "speaker_id": 38857,
          "reply_to": "M47",
          "text": "For the log, could we also have a field for who reported it? Sometimes we hear about things second-hand and it is hard to follow up.\nOn 'do not use', I have seen other yards use red tags on the steering wheel. Maybe we can do something similar and also put a red magnet on the board in A3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M50",
          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M47",
          "text": "I like the idea of red tags. For T11, we should also define clear criteria for when we use them, so we do not overuse or underuse.\nMaybe:\n- Any brake or steering issue.\n- Any major fluid leak.\n- Any safety equipment failure that affects safe operation, like no reversing alarm or serious lighting fault.\n- Any structural damage that could affect stability.\nIf one of these is found during the daily check in A1, we tag the vehicle and log it in A4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A1",
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M51",
          "speaker_id": 156061,
          "reply_to": "M47",
          "text": "For the near-miss you mentioned, I would log it as 'near-miss, hose still connected when driver tried to move'.\nIn A4, maybe we can add a simple checkbox for 'discussed in weekly review' so we know if we already talked about it in the T12 meeting.\nOn 'do not use', I agree with red steering wheel tags plus a mark on the board. We just need to be clear who is allowed to remove the tag once the issue is fixed.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987,
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M52",
          "speaker_id": 108987,
          "reply_to": "M50",
          "text": "The criteria you listed make sense. I just wonder about smaller issues like a cracked mirror. That is not as serious as brakes, but still important.\nShould we have a separate 'use with caution' note for those, or just log them in A4 and fix as soon as possible without tagging the vehicle?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            109283,
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M53",
          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": "M52",
          "text": "Good distinction.\nI would keep 'do not use' tags in T11 for issues that make the vehicle unsafe to operate at all, like the list 109283 shared.\nFor smaller but important issues like cracked mirrors or minor leaks, we log them in A4 and mark them as 'defect only' without tagging the vehicle, but we still set a due date for repair.\nThat way the log in A4 covers both incidents and defects, but the red tag is reserved for critical cases.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987,
            109283
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M54",
          "speaker_id": 38857,
          "reply_to": "M53",
          "text": "Who will be allowed to put and remove the red tags? I think it should not be everyone, or we might get confusion.\nMaybe only attendants and the fleet supervisor can put a 'do not use' tag, and only they can remove it after checking the repair.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126
          ]
        },

          "msg_id": "M55",
          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M54",
          "text": "I agree. We can write in T11 that attendants and the fleet supervisor are responsible for tagging and untagging.\nAlso, when we remove a tag, we should update A4 with the date and note that the vehicle is cleared, and change the status on the board in A3 from red back to normal.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A4",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38857,
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M56",

* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:
   * Messages where speaker_id == the participant’s _id.
   * If the participant speaks little, you can also use messages that mention them (mentions contains _id) as contextual evidence.
2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of HIGH => candidate HIGH
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of LOW  => candidate LOW
   * otherwise => MID
3. Attention:
   * If there are strong signals of HIGH and LOW at the same time for the same attribute, choose MID (conservative rule).
   * In the corporate context, everyone needs to deliver and demonstrate work; be careful to infer HIGH for something standard that should be MID.
   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:
   * If there are no messages from the participant, use MID for all three attributes and use evidence from a message where they were mentioned.

EVIDENCE RULES (MANDATORY)
* For each participant, return 2 to 5 items in evidence.
* Each evidence item:
  * attribute ∈ {"productivity","ability","performance"}
  * msg_id must exist in the channel
  * justification: one sentence justifying the label.
  * snippet must be a short quote (up to ~20 words) copied from the text of that msg (no comment).
* Do not invent msg_id.
* Do not include “LOW/MID/HIGH” in the snippet.

OUTPUT FORMAT (OUTPUT JSON SCHEMA)
{
  "predictions": [
    {
      "_id": 0,
      "productivity_level": "LOW|MID|HIGH",
      "ability_level": "LOW|MID|HIGH",
      "performance_level": "LOW|MID|HIGH",
      "justification": "string",
      "evidence": [
        {"attribute": "productivity|ability|performance", "msg_id": "M12", "snippet": "..."}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
FINAL
Return only the JSON in the schema above.

          "text": "Starting the training and pilot thread. You are an EVALUATOR that infers latent behavioral signals from Slack-style corporate conversations.
You do NOT have access to the true scenario labels. You must infer using ONLY:
* trajectory_signature / the participant’s trajectory and summarized history (to calibrate vocabulary and context);

CRITICAL OUTPUT RESTRICTIONS
* Return ONLY a single valid JSON object in the schema specified at the end.
* Do not include text outside the JSON.
* Do not use numbers (no score, no probability, no confidence).
* For each attribute, return ONLY one label in {LOW, MID, HIGH}.
* DETERMINISTIC RULE: if you are unsure/ambiguous, choose MID.
* Evidence snippets must be SHORT QUOTES from the text (no comments) and must NOT contain “LOW/MID/HIGH”.
* DO NOT use literal line breaks inside strings. If needed, use \n or if it is a tab use \t.
* Ensure quotes and braces are closed.

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:
   * Messages where speaker_id == the participant’s _id.
   * If the participant speaks little, you can also use messages that mention them (mentions contains _id) as contextual evidence.
2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:

   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

You are an EVALUATOR that infers latent behavioral signals from Slack-style corporate conversations.
You do NOT have access to the true scenario labels. You must infer using ONLY:
* trajectory_signature / the participant’s trajectory and summarized history (to calibrate vocabulary and context);
* the channel content and structure (messages + artifact_refs + decision_refs + thread_outcome).

CRITICAL OUTPUT RESTRICTIONS
* Return ONLY a single valid JSON object in the schema specified at the end.
* Do not include text outside the JSON.
* Do not use numbers (no score, no probability, no confidence).
* For each attribute, return ONLY one label in {LOW, MID, HIGH}.
* DETERMINISTIC RULE: if you are unsure/ambiguous, choose MID.
* Evidence snippets must be SHORT QUOTES from the text (no comments) and must NOT contain “LOW/MID/HIGH”.
* DO NOT use literal line breaks inside strings. If needed, use \n or if it is a tab use \t.
* Ensure quotes and braces are closed.

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

        "trajectory_summary": string,              # consolidated summary (may contain “->”)

IMPORTANT: You will use the participants' information [INPUT PARTICIPANTS] as a basis to try to infer the skill, productivity, and performance levels of each participant. Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:

          "speaker_id": 47214,

          "speaker_id": 421608,
          "reply_to": "M18",
          "text": "On the template in T2, could we include a field for hourly rate or salary reference, or is that too sensitive for the form?\nIf we do not include it, we need to be sure we can easily match the form to the correct rate in the system.\nAlso, for archiving in A3, I suggest we use a naming convention like year month type employee id, so that reconciliations are easier later.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T2",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449,
            107378
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M23",
          "speaker_id": 319449,
          "reply_to": "M19",
          "text": "For post, I would treat them as standard unless clearly marked urgent.\nWe can add a note in T4 that if a posted form is close to the cut off date, the clerk should flag it as urgent when logging it.\nI will also add a field in the log for the intake clerk, as suggested.\nOn the template, I prefer not to include salary figures, but we can require employee id and department so payroll can look up the rate.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T4",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            330756,
            107378,
            421608
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M24",
          "speaker_id": 330756,
          "reply_to": "M23",
          "text": "Got it.\nI will start marking late arriving post as urgent in the log when it is close to cut off.\nOnce T4 is final, I will keep it open on my screen when handling mail so I follow the same steps every time.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M25",
          "speaker_id": 107378,
          "reply_to": "M21",
          "text": "I support having a clear cut off time.\nMaybe we can say in T4 that urgent items for the current cycle must be logged and routed by noon on the cut off day, otherwise they move to the next cycle unless finance approves an exception.\nWe can then reflect that timing in the monthly checklist in A4 so it is consistent.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T4",
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449,
            408577
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 408577,
          "reply_to": "M25",
          "text": "Noon on cut off day works for me.\nIf we get anything after that, we can log it in A2 for the next cycle and note that it missed the cut off.\nThat will also help when we review issues after the pilot in A7.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A7",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            107378,
            319449
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 421608,
          "reply_to": "M25",
          "text": "Agree on the cut off and on not including salary figures in the template.\nAs long as employee id and department are mandatory fields in T2, we can link to the correct rate.\nFor archiving in T7, I will follow the naming convention you suggested so that payroll reports line up with the folders.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T2",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449,
            107378
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 319449,
          "reply_to": "M18",
          "text": "Let me summarise the routing rules for D3 based on this discussion:\n- All forms and emails are logged by the intake clerk with date, time, employee id, department, and whether they are urgent.\n- Standard items are scanned and saved using the A3 naming convention, then routed to the generic payroll inbox.\n- Urgent items for the current cycle must be logged and routed by noon on cut off day, plus an email with 'urgent' in the subject.\n- Items received after the cut off move to the next cycle unless finance approves an exception.\n- Posted items follow the same rules; if they arrive close to cut off, the clerk marks them urgent in the log.\nIf there are no objections, I will mark these as the approved routing rules in T4 and A3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T4",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            330756,
            107378,
            408577,
            421608
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 107378,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "Summary looks good.\nFor the templates in T2, I propose we finalise the absence and overtime form with these mandatory fields: employee id, department, dates, hours, type of absence or overtime, manager approval, and indicator if it affects previous periods.\nCost centre can be optional if it matches department.\nIf everyone agrees, we can treat this as the final version for D4 and use it in the quick reference guide A6 and T9.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T2",
            "A6",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D4"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            319449,
            408577,
            421608,
            330756
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M30",
          "speaker_id": 330756,
          "reply_to": "M29",
          "text": "I am comfortable using that template.\nHaving clear mandatory fields will make it easier at the front desk to check forms before we log them.\nNo further changes from me.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M31",
          "speaker_id": 408577,
          "reply_to": "M29",
          "text": "Template fields work for payroll.\nWith employee id and department, we can link to rates and cost centres on our side.\nI will make sure the monthly checklist in A4 references the routing cut off and the use of this template.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T3",
            "T2"
          ],

          "mentions": [
            107378

        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M32",
          "speaker_id": 421608,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "No objections from me on D3 and D4.\nOnce T7 is updated with the folder structure and examples, I will test a couple of months of data to see if the routing and archiving work smoothly together.",

        {
          "msg_id": "M33",
          "speaker_id": 107378,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Opening the confidentiality and escalation thread.\nI have drafted a first version of the confidentiality and access guideline in T6, and a basic escalation path for discrepancies in T11.\nThese will feed into A5 and A8.\nPlease review and share any concerns, especially around who can see what, and how we handle wage or hours discrepancies raised by staff.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T6",
            "T11",
            "A5",
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            408577,
            421608,
            319449,
            330756
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M34",
          "speaker_id": 408577,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "In T6, I see three access levels proposed:\n1) Full access for payroll clerks and HR to detailed payroll records.\n2) Limited access for office clerks to routing logs and high level status only.\n3) Read only access for finance to summaries and reconciliations.\nThis makes sense to me, but we should be explicit that office clerks should not open or store files with full salary details unless strictly needed for routing.\nMaybe we can add a rule that any such files are handled only by payroll or HR.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T6",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            107378,
            319449,
            330756
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M35",
          "speaker_id": 421608,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "I agree with the three access levels.\nFor A5, we should also cover how long we keep documents and where backups are stored.\nFor example, detailed payroll records kept for a set number of years in the secure archive, and logs in A2 kept for a shorter period.\nOn escalation in T11, I would like to see clear response times, such as two working days for initial response and five working days for resolution where possible.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A2",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            107378
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 319449,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "From the office side, I support limiting access to detailed salary data.\nWe mainly need to see whether a form has been received, logged, and processed, not the actual amounts.\nIn A6 and the training outline, we can emphasise that any documents with full pay details should be sealed or marked confidential and passed directly to payroll without copying.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "T12",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            330756,
            107378
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M37",
          "speaker_id": 330756,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "That helps.\nSometimes staff hand me envelopes with payslips or letters from external agencies.\nI was not always sure if I should open them.\nWith this guideline, I will treat anything marked confidential as for payroll or HR only and just log that I passed it on, without opening it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 107378,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "On retention, I can add to T6 that:\n- Detailed payroll records are stored in the secure archive for the required number of years.\n- Routing logs and issue logs in A2 and A7 are kept for a shorter period, enough to support audits and reviews.\nFor escalation in T11, I propose three scenarios: incorrect hours, incorrect rate, and missing payment.\nEach would have an initial response within two working days and target resolution within five working days, with clear contacts at each step.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T6",
            "A2",
            "A7",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            421608,
            408577
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 408577,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "For the escalation path in T11, I suggest this order:\n1) Staff contact office clerk or payroll inbox.\n2) Office clerk logs the query in A2 and forwards to payroll.\n3) Payroll reviews and, if needed, escalates to HR or finance.\n4) If not resolved within the target time, it goes to the finance manager.\nWe should also note in A8 that any adjustments after payroll close must be documented and, where needed, approved by finance before processing.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A2",
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            107378,
            319449
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M40",
          "speaker_id": 421608,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "That sequence works.\nI would only add that for missing payments, we should check the bank file and confirmation step in A1 before assuming an error in the payroll calculation.\nIf the payment was rejected by the bank, the escalation should include contacting the bank or finance to resolve it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            408577,
            107378
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M41",
          "speaker_id": 319449,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "From the office perspective, it is helpful to have clear response times and to know when to follow up.\nIn A6, we can include a short section explaining to clerks how to log queries in A2 and when to escalate if staff come back asking for updates.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "A2",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            330756
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M42",
          "speaker_id": 330756,
          "reply_to": "M41",
          "text": "Yes, having that written down will help a lot.\nRight now I sometimes promise staff I will check and then I am not sure who to ask.\nWith A8 and the log in A2, I can follow the same steps every time.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M43",
          "speaker_id": 107378,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "Let me summarise the confidentiality and access rules for D5:\n- Payroll clerks and HR have full access to detailed payroll records.\n- Office clerks have access only to routing logs and high level status, not to detailed salary data, except when strictly needed for routing.\n- Finance has read only access to summaries and reconciliations.\n- Documents marked confidential are passed directly to payroll or HR without being opened by office clerks.\n- Retention periods are defined for detailed records and logs, with storage in secure archives.\nIf everyone is aligned, I will update T6 and A5 accordingly.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T6",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D5"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            408577,
            421608,
            319449,
            330756
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M44",
          "speaker_id": 408577,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "I am aligned with that summary.\nFor D6, I suggest we formalise the escalation path in A8 and T11 as:\n1) Staff raise discrepancy via office clerk or payroll inbox.\n2) Office clerk logs it in A2 and forwards to payroll.\n3) Payroll investigates and, if needed, involves HR or finance.\n4) If not resolved within five working days, it escalates to the finance manager.\n5) Any adjustments after payroll close are documented and approved by finance before processing.\nIf there are no objections, we can treat this as the agreed standard path.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "T11",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D6"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            107378,
            319449,
            421608,
            330756
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M45",
          "speaker_id": 421608,
          "reply_to": "M44",
          "text": "No objections from me on D5 and D6.\nI will make sure the monthly checklist in A4 includes a step to review open discrepancies in A2 before we close payroll.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            107378,
            408577
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M46",
          "speaker_id": 319449,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "All good from the office side.\nI will reflect the confidentiality rules and escalation steps in the training outline in T12 and in the quick reference guide A6 so clerks know exactly what to do.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T12",
            "A6",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            330756
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M47",
          "speaker_id": 330756,
          "reply_to": "M44",
          "text": "I am clear on the rules and the escalation path now.\nI will start logging staff queries in A2 as described and follow the steps in A8 when people come to the desk with concerns about their pay.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319449
          ]
        }

          "msg_id": "M48",
          "speaker_id": 408577,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Time to plan the pilot payroll cycle using the new workflow.\nWe need to confirm which cycle we will use for the pilot and what success looks like.\nI have started T8 with a draft plan and updated T5 with a first version of the shared tracking sheet that links to A2.\nPlease confirm readiness and share any concerns before we lock in dates.",
          "artifact_refs": [
