        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M23",
          "speaker_id": 72802,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "Thanks for sharing the outline.\n\nOn the academic side for T9, I think we should explicitly link internship activities to learning outcomes such as communication with guests, teamwork, and understanding of hospitality operations.\n\nI am not entirely sure how detailed we need to be in A2 versus a separate mapping document, so I would appreciate guidance from 45096 on how much detail is typical in such frameworks.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T9",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968,
            45096
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M24",
          "speaker_id": 45096,
          "reply_to": "M23",
          "text": "For A2, I would keep the learning outcomes at a moderate level of detail: a short list of core competencies the internship should support.\n\nThen, in T9, we can create a separate mapping document that links specific hotel tasks to programme learning outcomes and credit or recognition options.\n\nThis way, the framework stays readable for non-specialists, and we still have enough detail for academic approval.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72802,
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M25",
          "speaker_id": 36727,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "From the research side, I suggest we integrate a short section in A2 on monitoring and evaluation, pointing to A5.\n\nWe can specify that all internships will include a pre and post survey and, where feasible, a short debrief interview. This will help normalise data collection for hotels and students.\n\nI can draft a paragraph for that section once I have the first version of the evaluation questions under T4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A5",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968,
            45096
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 19278,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "Looking at the structure, I would recommend that A2 clearly distinguishes between tasks interns can do independently and tasks they can only do under supervision.\n\nThis will make it easier later to align A3 and the checklists in A7 with the framework.\n\nWe should also mention in the safeguards that interns will receive a basic orientation on accessibility and inclusion, so they are prepared to interact respectfully with diverse guests and colleagues.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A7",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968,
            36727
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 497314,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "For A2, could we also include a short section on communication principles that will later be expanded in A6?\n\nFor example, commitments to clear language, avoiding stereotypes, and ensuring that all public materials explain the support available to interns.\n\nThis will help keep T6 and T8 aligned with the framework from the start.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A6",
            "T6",
            "T8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 52968,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "These are good points. I will adjust the outline of A2 to include:\n\n- A section on task categories (independent vs supervised), to be detailed later in A3 and A7.\n- A short monitoring and evaluation section referencing A5.\n- A brief communication principles section that links to A6.\n\nBefore I lock the structure for D3, are there any concerns about the proposed duration, roles, or safeguards that we have not yet covered?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A7",
            "A5",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            19278,
            36727,
            45096,
            72802,
            497314
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 72802,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "No additional concerns from me on duration or roles.\n\nFor safeguards, I would just ask that we explicitly mention that participation is voluntary and that students can withdraw without academic penalty, as long as they follow a simple procedure.\n\nThis will be important when we later explain the programme in the student training outline for A4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M30",
          "speaker_id": 45096,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "I agree with the structure you described.\n\nOn roles, could we clarify in A2 that the university coordinator is responsible for ensuring that internship tasks remain aligned with academic requirements and that any changes are documented? That will make T9 easier to maintain over time.\n\nOtherwise, I am comfortable moving towards confirming the framework structure for D3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M31",
          "speaker_id": 19278,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "From the hotel side, the proposed duration and roles look workable.\n\nI would just add that the framework should state that hotels can request adjustments to intern schedules during exceptional peak periods, in coordination with the university coordinator.\n\nThis will help avoid friction later and can be reflected in both A3 and the daily checklists in A7.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A7",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M32",
          "speaker_id": 36727,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "No objections from me.\n\nI will make sure that the evaluation tools in A5 reflect the roles and safeguards described in A2, so that we can later see whether they are working as intended.\n\nOnce you have a near-final structure, please share it so I can align T4 accordingly.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A2",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M33",
          "speaker_id": 52968,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "Based on your feedback, I propose we confirm the structure of the internship framework for D3 as follows:\n\n- Section 1: Objectives and scope of the pilot.\n- Section 2: Duration and schedule (8 to 10 weeks, 10 to 12 hours per week, with flexibility for peak periods).\n- Section 3: Roles and responsibilities (students, hotel supervisors, university coordinator, policy contact).\n- Section 4: Safeguards and compliance (working time, insurance, non-discrimination, voluntary participation, withdrawal process).\n- Section 5: Task categories (independent vs supervised), to be detailed in A3 and A7.\n- Section 6: Monitoring and evaluation overview, referencing A5.\n- Section 7: Communication principles, referencing A6.\n\nIf there are no strong objections, I will proceed with this structure for A2 under T2.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A7",
            "A5",
            "A6",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            72802,
            45096,
            36727,
            19278,
            497314
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M34",
          "speaker_id": 72802,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "This structure works for me, and it gives us a clear place to connect academic requirements later.\n\nFor D3, I support confirming this framework outline.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M35",
          "speaker_id": 45096,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "I also support this structure for D3.\n\nOnce you have a draft of A2, I can review the safeguards and roles sections to ensure they are consistent with typical academic and ethical expectations.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 497314,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "From a communication angle, this structure is clear and gives us a solid base for A6.\n\nI agree with confirming it for D3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M37",
          "speaker_id": 19278,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "No objections from me. The explicit task categories and flexibility for peak periods are especially important for hotels.\n\nSo I am fine with confirming D3 as you summarised it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 72802,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "On mapping internship activities to academic requirements for D4, I propose the following approach for T9:\n\n- We define 4 to 5 core learning outcomes in A2.\n- For each outcome, we list typical hotel tasks (from A3 and A7) that contribute to it.\n- We then specify how many hours or types of tasks are needed for students to receive credit or a certificate.\n\nDoes this sound reasonable, or are we overcomplicating it for a pilot?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T9",
            "A3",
            "A7",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            45096,
            19278
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 45096,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "I think this is a good and manageable approach for D4.\n\nFor the pilot, we can keep the mapping relatively simple: for example, specify that completing the internship with satisfactory feedback on key tasks corresponds to a certain number of hours of practical training or a pass or fail recognition.\n\nWe can refine the granularity later if the programme is scaled up.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72802
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M40",
          "speaker_id": 36727,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "From an evaluation perspective, a simple mapping is easier to monitor.\n\nIf we define a small set of learning outcomes and link them to observable tasks, we can design A5 to capture whether students actually had the chance to perform those tasks and how confident they felt.\n\nSo I support your proposal for D4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T4",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72802
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M41",
          "speaker_id": 19278,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "This mapping approach is workable from the hotel side as long as we do not create a very complex tracking system for supervisors.\n\nIf we can keep it to a short checklist linked to A7, supervisors can quickly confirm which tasks interns have practiced, which will then feed into the academic recognition under T9.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A7",
            "T3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72802
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M42",
          "speaker_id": 52968,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "Let me capture D4 based on this discussion.\n\nFor the pilot, we will map internship activities to academic requirements by: defining a small set of core learning outcomes in A2, linking them to typical hotel tasks described in A3 and A7, and recognising completion through a simple pass or fail or fixed credit equivalent, based on supervisor checklists and student reflection.\n\nI will reflect this approach in the relevant section of A2 and leave the detailed mapping document to T9.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A7",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [

        {
          "msg_id": "M43",
          "speaker_id": 19278,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I am sharing a first draft list of feasible intern tasks and daily routines from the hotel side, which will feed into A3, A7, T3 and T11.\n\nProposed task categories:\n\nFront-of-house (mostly supervised at first):\n- Greeting guests in the lobby and directing them to reception.\n- Assisting with simple check-in or check-out steps under staff guidance.\n- Helping prepare welcome materials and information stands.\n\nBack-of-house (some independent, some supervised):\n- Preparing and restocking housekeeping trolleys.\n- Sorting laundry and amenities.\n- Supporting simple breakfast prep tasks that do not involve sharp tools or hot surfaces.\n\nI have also started listing common operational risks (for example, slips and falls, data privacy at reception, guest complaints) and basic mitigation steps for T11.\n\nPlease react with what feels realistic, what should be removed, and what we might be missing.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A7",
            "T3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            36727,
            52968,
            72802,
            45096,
            497314
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M44",
          "speaker_id": 36727,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "This looks like a solid starting point.\n\nFrom a research and inclusion angle, I would suggest we also consider tasks that allow interns to interact with diverse guests in a structured way, for example supporting information desks or feedback collection, as long as they are trained.\n\nFor T11, could you share more detail on how you see data privacy risks at reception and what simple rules we can include in A3 so interns do not accidentally see or share sensitive information?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            19278
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M45",
          "speaker_id": 52968,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "Thanks for structuring this so clearly.\n\nFrom a regulatory perspective, we should avoid assigning interns to tasks that could be interpreted as full responsibility for cash handling, security, or unsupervised night shifts.\n\nIn A3, could we mark such tasks as explicitly excluded for interns, so that hotels do not accidentally cross a line when implementing the pilot?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            19278
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M46",
          "speaker_id": 72802,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "Looking at these tasks from an academic perspective, they align well with learning outcomes around communication, teamwork, and understanding hotel operations.\n\nFor T9, it would help if we can group tasks into a few clusters, such as guest interaction, operational support, and back-of-house logistics. That will make it easier to map them to learning outcomes later.\n\nI do not see any major issues, but I am less familiar with the operational risks, so I will rely on you and 36727 to flag anything critical for T11.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T9",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            19278,
            36727
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M47",
          "speaker_id": 45096,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "I agree this is a good starting list.\n\nFor inclusion, we might want to ensure that there are tasks suitable for students with different physical or sensory needs. For example, some roles could focus more on coordination, documentation, or digital tasks rather than physical work.\n\nCould we add a note in A3 that hotels should, where possible, offer at least one lower-physical-intensity task option per intern?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            19278
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M48",
          "speaker_id": 497314,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "From a communication standpoint, it will be important that the tasks we list in A3 and A7 are easy to explain to students and hotel staff.\n\nOnce you have a more detailed draft, I can help simplify the wording for non-specialists under T8, so that the checklists are clear and do not feel intimidating.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A7",
            "T8",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            19278
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M49",
          "speaker_id": 19278,
          "reply_to": "M44",
          "text": "On data privacy at reception, the main risks are interns seeing full ID documents, credit card details, or sensitive notes in the system.\n\nIn A3, I propose we include simple rules such as: interns do not handle payment cards, do not read or enter sensitive notes, and only observe or assist with non-sensitive parts of check-in, like confirming breakfast times or explaining facilities.\n\nFor T11, I will list data privacy as a specific risk with these mitigation steps.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            36727,
            52968
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M50",
          "speaker_id": 19278,
          "reply_to": "M45",
          "text": "Agreed on excluding cash handling, security, and unsupervised night shifts.\n\nI will create a short list of explicitly excluded tasks in A3 and mirror that in the risk section for T11, so hotels have a clear red line.\n\nThis will also help us communicate to students what they should not be asked to do.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [

          "text": "I am sharing draft key messages and a communication plan outline for A6 under T6.\n\nKey messages (for students, hotels, and public):\n- The programme offers structured, supported internships in hospitality for students from diverse backgrounds.\n- Hotels and universities work together to ensure fair conditions, learning opportunities, and respect for all participants.\n- The pilot is small-scale and evidence-based, with clear monitoring through A5 and a summary in A8.\n\nChannels:\n- Internal: university mailing lists, student support channels, and direct outreach to partner hotels.\n- External: a short web article, social media posts, and possibly a local press note once the pilot is underway.\n\nI would like your feedback on tone, missing points, and which channels we should prioritise before we sign off on D8.",

          "text": "Thanks for drafting this.\n\nFrom a policy perspective, I would like the messages to emphasise that the programme complies with education and labour regulations and that it is a partnership, not a replacement for regular staff.\n\nFor channels, I suggest we prioritise internal university and hotel communications first, and only move to broader media once the pilot is running smoothly.",

I will update A1 to include: 1) a simple rule for placing heavy pallets over the axles and keeping weight balanced left to right, and 2) a clear check that pallets are staged correctly before loading, as suggested by 66233. For unloading, I will add a step to verify labels and delivery notes before moving items off the truck, as 18459 mentioned.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341,
            66233,
            18459
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M25",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M20",
          "text": "On A2, I will add: 1) corner protectors and double-walled cartons as mandatory for certain fragile categories, 2) a maximum stack height for mixed cartons, and 3) a rule that any stack above that height must be wrapped to the pallet. I will also add a short note that special cargo and animals follow A5 and should not be stacked or packed like standard goods.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A5",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            59367,
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 297341,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "Can we also clarify in A1 when to use straps versus load bars or nets? Right now the draft says secure the load, but does not say how to choose between options. Maybe a simple table or rule based on weight and type of goods would help.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 59367,
          "reply_to": "M25",
          "text": "For bulky items, the draft in A2 says to avoid overhang, but maybe we should be stricter: no overhang beyond the pallet footprint, and if the item is taller than it is wide, it must be strapped directly to the pallet. That would reduce the wobble we see with tall furniture pieces.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045,
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 18459,
          "reply_to": "M25",
          "text": "In the pre-departure checklist from A7, could we add a simple reminder to check that fragile labels are visible from the aisle? Sometimes they end up facing the wall and we forget to handle them more carefully during unloading.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A7",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "I will add a small decision table in A1: straps for most palletised loads, load bars for blocking rows, and nets for irregular or mixed loose items, with examples. I will also integrate the no-overhang and tall-item rules for bulky goods into A2 as suggested by 59367, and the visible fragile label check into the A7-based checklist.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A7",
            "T2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341,
            59367,
            18459
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M30",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M23",
          "text": "Thanks for including references to A5. As long as A1 clearly says that animals and sensitive cargo follow a separate mandatory guide and must be loaded in designated zones, I am comfortable with the core SOP being approved now and we can refine the special handling details in TH4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A5",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M31",
          "speaker_id": 297341,
          "reply_to": "M29",
          "text": "From my side, with these updates, the core loading and unloading steps in A1 look solid and practical. I am ok to treat this as our standard, assuming we can still tweak wording later if pilots show something unexpected.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M32",
          "speaker_id": 59367,
          "reply_to": "M29",
          "text": "I am also comfortable with the packing rules for fragile and bulky items in A2 now: clear materials, stack height limits, and no-overhang rule. That should cut down on crushed boxes and wobbly loads.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M33",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M31",
          "text": "Great, I will freeze the current version of A1 with the updated core steps and the decision table for securing loads, and A2 with the agreed fragile and bulky packing rules. We can still refine examples and visuals later, but the main process is now set for the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [

        {
          "msg_id": "M34",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have drafted a proposed shelf map and labelling scheme for the main city depot in A3, based on T4. Zones are grouped by route and load sequence, with clear flow paths from inbound to staging to loading bays. Aisles and shelves follow a simple code so new staff can find items quickly. Please review and tell me if this works from the loading and special cargo perspectives before we pick the version for the pilot depot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341,
            38045,
            59367,
            18459,
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M35",
          "speaker_id": 297341,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "Looking at A3, I like that the fast-moving items are closest to the loading bays. One concern: the current map has returns and damaged goods in a corner near the main flow path. Could we move that zone slightly away so it does not block pallet jacks during peak times?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "From a mover point of view, the route-based zoning in A3 is helpful. Could we also mark a clear staging strip for each bay where pallets must be aligned and facing the right way before loading? That would tie in nicely with the SOP in A1 and reduce turning pallets inside the truck.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A1",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233,
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M37",
          "speaker_id": 18459,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "The labelling codes look clear, but I am not sure how we will handle temporary overflow when a zone is full. Should we have a standard overflow area with its own label so we do not just park pallets in the aisles?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 59367,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "I like the simple aisle-shelf numbering. For tall or bulky items, could we reserve lower shelves in certain aisles and mark them clearly? That would avoid putting heavy or awkward pieces up high where they are harder to handle safely.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "For animals and sensitive cargo, I see a dedicated zone on the map, but it is not fully separated from general freight. Could we add a buffer area or at least ensure that noisy or unstable loads are not staged right next to that zone?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A5",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M40",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "Good catch. I can move the returns and damaged goods zone one aisle over and mark a clear boundary so it does not spill into the main flow path. I will also add a standard overflow area with its own label, as 18459 suggested, so we avoid blocking aisles.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341,
            18459
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M41",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "I will add marked staging strips in front of each loading bay, with labels that match the route codes. That way, pallets are aligned and oriented correctly before loading, and movers can follow the sequence from A1 more easily.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A1",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M42",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "For bulky and heavy items, I will reserve lower shelves in specific aisles and mark them with a clear icon so staff know those positions are for heavy or awkward loads only. That should reduce risky lifts and awkward reaches.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            59367
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M43",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "On the special cargo zone, I will add a buffer strip and mark adjacent shelves as low-noise, low-vibration only. We can also add a simple sign reminding staff not to stage unstable or noisy loads next to that area.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A5",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M44",
          "speaker_id": 297341,
          "reply_to": "M41",
          "text": "With these tweaks, the layout looks workable for the pilot. The route-based zones, staging strips, and clear overflow area should cut down on confusion and last-minute reshuffling.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M45",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M41",
          "text": "Agreed. From a mover perspective, I am comfortable using this version of A3 as the standard for the main city depot pilot. For the regional depot, we can mirror the same scheme with minor adjustments for size.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233,
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M46",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "With the buffer and low-noise marking around the special cargo zone, I am ok to go ahead and test this layout in the pilot depot. We can fine-tune details after we see how it works in practice.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A5",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M47",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M45",
          "text": "Thanks all. I will lock this version of A3 as the storage layout and labelling scheme for the main city depot pilot and prepare a scaled version for the regional depot. We will capture feedback during the pilot under T9 and adjust if needed.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T4",
            "T9"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D5"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            297341,

        {
          "msg_id": "M48",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have drafted the animal and sensitive cargo handling guide in A5 based on T5. It covers: types of animals and sensitive goods we move, welfare and handling requirements, loading and unloading order, separation from general freight, and responsibilities for checks during loading and short stops. Please review and let me know what needs clarification before we confirm the mandatory steps.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341,
            38045,
            59367,
            18459,
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M49",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M48",
          "text": "In A5 you mention that animals should be loaded last and unloaded first, with a buffer zone. Could we make it explicit how far they should be from noisy or unstable loads, and whether we ever allow stacking anything on top of animal crates? Right now it just says avoid stacking, which some might interpret loosely.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M50",
          "speaker_id": 297341,
          "reply_to": "M48",
          "text": "For sensitive cargo like medical supplies or temperature-sensitive goods, do we have clear rules in A5 about where to place them in the truck and how often to check them during loading and short stops? It would help to tie that to the pre-departure checklist in A7.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A7",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M51",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M48",
          "text": "On the depot side, we should align A5 with the special cargo zone in A3. For example, the guide could say that animals and sensitive goods must be staged only in that zone and never in general aisles, even temporarily. That will avoid confusion when we are busy.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A3",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M52",
          "speaker_id": 18459,
          "reply_to": "M48",
          "text": "I have a question on responsibilities: in A5, who is supposed to do the welfare checks during loading? Is it the driver, a groom, or any mover assigned to that route? It would help to have that spelled out so we do not assume someone else is doing it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520,
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M53",
          "speaker_id": 59367,
          "reply_to": "M48",
          "text": "For sensitive equipment, could we add a rule that they must be secured with non-slip mats or similar, not just placed on top of other boxes? I have seen some delicate items slide when we brake, even if they were not very heavy.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M54",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M49",
          "text": "Good points. I will update A5 to say: 1) no stacking on top of animal crates or cages, under any circumstances, and 2) a minimum buffer distance from noisy or unstable loads, plus a rule that such loads must be secured and placed away from the animal zone. I will also reference the securing rules from A1 so we stay consistent.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A1",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M55",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M50",
          "text": "For temperature-sensitive and medical goods, I will add in A5: 1) preferred placement away from doors and direct heat sources, 2) a requirement to check seals and indicators before loading and at the first short stop, and 3) a link to the pre-departure checklist in A7 so these checks are not skipped.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A7",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M56",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M51",
          "text": "I will align A5 with the special cargo zone in A3: animals and sensitive goods must be staged only in that zone, never in general aisles or overflow. I will also clarify that if the zone is full, loading must pause and the supervisor decides on the next step, rather than improvising.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A3",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            66233
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M57",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M52",
          "text": "On responsibilities, I will specify in A5 that: 1) during loading, a named person (driver or groom, depending on the route) is responsible for welfare and condition checks, and 2) this name must be written on the load sheet. That way, there is no doubt about who is doing the checks.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18459,
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M58",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M53",
          "text": "For sensitive equipment, I will add a rule in A5 that they must be placed on non-slip surfaces or mats and secured, not just stacked on other boxes. I will cross-reference the packing materials guidance in A2 so we use the right supports.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A2",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            59367
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M59",
          "speaker_id": 297341,
          "reply_to": "M55",
          "text": "With these updates, the steps in A5 look clear and practical from my side. The links to A1, A2, A3, and A7 help keep everything consistent with the rest of the process.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M60",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M54",
          "text": "I am comfortable treating the updated A5 as mandatory for any route carrying animals or sensitive cargo. The no-stacking rule and clear responsibilities should prevent most of the issues we have seen.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M61",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M56",
          "text": "From the depot side, I am aligned. We can implement the special zone rules from A5 in the pilot depots without extra equipment, just clearer markings and training.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A3",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M62",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M60",
          "text": "Thanks all. I will finalise A5 with these clarifications and mark the steps as mandatory for any route or depot handling animals or sensitive cargo. We can still refine examples after the pilot, but the core requirements are now set.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D6"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            297341,
            38045,
            59367,
            18459,
            66233
          ]
        }
      ],
      "thread_outcome": {
        "decisions_made": [
          "D6"
        ],
        "next_steps": [
          {
            "task_id": "T5",

    {
      "thread_id": "TH5",
      "messages": [
        {
          "msg_id": "M63",
          "speaker_id": 297341,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Time to line up the pilot. Proposal: we run a one-week pilot on two depots (main city and regional) and two routes (one mixed-goods, one with regular animals or sensitive cargo). We will use A1, A2, A3, A5, and the pre-departure checklist from A7. I have started T6 for the training checklist, T8 for the pilot plan, T11 for KPIs, and T12 for quick visual aids. Please review the draft plan and suggest changes before we confirm routes, dates, and KPIs.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A5",
            "A7",
            "T6",
            "T8",
            "T11",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045,
            59367,
            18459,
            66233,
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M64",
          "speaker_id": 38045,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "On routes: I suggest we pick the main city to north suburb route as the mixed-goods pilot, and the main city to farm belt route for animals and sensitive cargo. Both are busy enough to give us data but not the most overloaded ones, so we can afford a bit of learning time.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341,
            265520
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M65",
          "speaker_id": 265520,
          "reply_to": "M64",
          "text": "I am fine with the farm belt route as the special cargo pilot. It has a good mix of animals and other sensitive goods, and the teams there are used to some extra checks already, so they should adapt quickly to A5.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38045,
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M66",
          "speaker_id": 66233,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "For training, I propose we run short on-floor sessions in each pilot depot: 1) a walkthrough of A1, A2, A3, and A5 using A4 as the checklist, and 2) a quick tour of the new zones and labels. We can do this in 30 minutes per shift without disrupting the schedule.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A5",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M67",
          "speaker_id": 59367,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "On KPIs for T11, I would track at least: 1) number of damaged items per 100 deliveries, 2) number of loading-related delays over 15 minutes, and 3) number of reported incidents or near-misses. A6 already has a structure we can reuse for the tracking sheet.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            297341
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M68",

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.

          "speaker_id": 390795,
          "reply_to": "M58",
          "text": "For me, option 1 feels closest to what we already have in the store, so it will not look out of place.\nI am a bit worried that a light panel might show dust more quickly, which would mean more cleaning in A3.",

            448438

          "text": "From the farmer side, a single entry point with someone doing quick triage would feel simpler. WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Sharing the first draft of the waste tracking template and routine for feedback.\n\nI have created a simple version of the Food Waste Baseline and KPI Tracker (A1) tailored for daily use in the three pilot units, and a short Standard Operating Procedure for Food Waste Tracking (A2).\n\nKey points:\n- Daily sheet: records item, quantity wasted, reason (prep error, overproduction, expired, plate waste), and estimated cost\n- Weekly summary: auto-calculates total waste cost and percentage vs food cost\n- Routine: kitchen lead fills in the sheet at end of each shift; manager reviews weekly and logs into A1\n\nThis is linked to T3 and will also feed into the staff training materials for T7.\n\nI would appreciate your comments on:\n- is the level of detail manageable for staff?\n- which KPIs from A1 should be visible in the executive dashboard (A7) for T9?\n\nPlease share any changes you think are needed before we test this in one pilot unit for three days, as required by T3.",

          "reply_to": "M13",
          "text": "Thanks for putting this together.\n\nOn the template:\n- The daily sheet structure looks good. I would add a simple category field (protein, veg, starch, dessert, other) so we can quickly see where the biggest issues are.\n- For reasons, maybe we can pre-define a short list with codes to speed up entry and reduce free text.\n\nOn KPIs for A7 and T9, I suggest we start with:\n- waste cost as a percentage of food cost per unit\n- waste per cover (in cost)\n- top 5 items by waste cost\n\nThese are easy to explain to managers and will help us later when we design the menu and sales playbook (A4).",

          "speaker_id": 332110,

          "text": "From a purchasing perspective, the template is a good start.\n\nTo make T4 easier later, I would like to see:\n- a link between each waste line and the supplier or at least the product group\n- a flag for items that were over-ordered vs items that were produced but not sold\n\nThis will help us identify high-waste categories and adjust order frequency and minimum order quantities in line with A3.\n\nFor the executive dashboard (A7), I would also recommend a simple view of waste by product group, so we can see if changes in purchasing are having the expected effect.",

          "reply_to": "M13",
          "text": "Looking at this with the dashboard in mind.\n\nFor A7 and T9, I would like the following KPIs to be available at least weekly:\n- waste cost percentage vs food cost, by unit and overall\n- trend over time (even if we only have a few weeks at first)\n- top waste reasons (overproduction, prep error, expiry, plate waste)\n\nWe should keep the number of KPIs small at the beginning so that unit managers do not feel overwhelmed.\n\nOn the routine: do you think managers will have enough time to review weekly and log into A1, or should we consider a bi-weekly review at first to reduce the load?",

Weekly feels like a good compromise, but we need to keep the process simple.\n\nMaybe we can:\n- keep the daily entries very light, as in the draft\n- have a short weekly review (15 minutes) where the manager looks at the summary and notes one or two actions\n\nIf we agree on this, we can lock in the weekly reporting cadence for T3 and T9 and reflect it in A2 and A7.",

          "text": "Before we move ahead, I want to be sure we are all aligned that this template and routine will be our standard for the pilot.\n\nTo summarize the current version:\n- daily entries with item, quantity, category, reason code, avoidable vs unavoidable, product group\n- weekly summary with waste cost percentage vs food cost, waste per cover, top 5 items by waste cost, waste by product group\n- weekly manager review and logging into A1\n\nIf everyone is ok, we will:\n- approve this as the standard waste tracking template and reporting cadence for the pilot (T3)\n- test it in one pilot unit for three days starting early next week, then roll out to the other two pilot units if no major issues appear\n\nPlease react or comment today so we can close this and move on.",

          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 332110,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Sharing initial analysis of high-waste categories and proposed purchasing changes for the three pilot units.\n\nUsing the early entries in A1 and the process maps from T2, I have identified the following high-waste categories:\n- fresh herbs and salad greens\n- bakery items (bread and pastries)\n- pre-cut fruit\n\nKey drivers seem to be over-ordering for weekends and unpredictable demand.\n\nMy proposal for T4, to be captured in the Purchasing and Inventory Adjustment Guidelines (A3):\n1) Fresh herbs and salad greens\n- reduce order quantities by 15 percent for weekdays\n- increase order frequency from twice to three times per week where suppliers allow\n2) Bakery items\n- shift part of the volume to a supplier that offers smaller batch deliveries (see A6)\n- introduce a standing rule to freeze surplus bread at end of day where food safety allows\n3) Pre-cut fruit\n- tighten par levels based on last 4 weeks of sales\n- introduce a rule to only order pre-cut for weekends and use whole fruit during weekdays\n\nFor T5, I have also drafted a list of top 5 suppliers for perishable goods in A6, with notes on which ones already offer flexible quantities or schedules.\n\nI would like your feedback on:\n- any operational risks you see with these changes\n- which suppliers we should prioritize for more flexible delivery terms.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A3",
            "A6",
            "T2",
            "T4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [

            412987,

        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 66412,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "Thanks for the breakdown.\n\nFrom the units side, a few points:\n- Increasing delivery frequency for greens is helpful, but we need to check storage capacity in Airport Express. They are tight on space.\n- Freezing surplus bread is possible in City Center Bistro and Riverside Grill, but we need clear guidance on what is acceptable from a food safety perspective.\n- Switching pre-cut fruit to whole fruit on weekdays might require some extra prep time in the kitchen.\n\nI do not see major blockers, but we should pilot these changes in just one unit first before applying them to all three, to avoid stock-outs or quality issues.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A6",
            "T4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            332110

        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 412987,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "On the sales and guest side:\n- For bakery items, we need to be careful that freezing does not affect quality for breakfast guests. Maybe we can limit frozen bread to toast and keep fresh for premium items.\n- For pre-cut fruit, guests at Airport Express expect speed. Using whole fruit on weekdays might slow service unless we adjust prep routines.\n\nI suggest we:\n- test the bakery and fruit changes first in Riverside Grill, where service pressure is a bit lower\n- monitor guest feedback and waste data in A1 closely during the first two weeks.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          "speaker_id": 492953,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "From a risk perspective, I want to make sure we do not breach any existing supplier contracts and that we stay within food safety rules.\n\nOn A6, do we have clarity on minimum order quantities and delivery frequency clauses for the current suppliers? If not, we should double-check before we commit to changes in T4.\n\nFor T5, I would prioritize suppliers where:\n- we already have a good relationship\n- they have some flexibility in their logistics\n\nCan you suggest which two or three suppliers from the top 5 in A6 we should approach first?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",

          "decision_refs": [],

          "msg_id": "M30",
          "speaker_id": 332110,
          "reply_to": "M29",
          "text": "On A6, I have checked the contracts for the top 5 perishable suppliers.\n\nSummary:\n- Supplier 1 (greens and herbs): minimum order quantity is moderate, but they already deliver three times per week to some units. They are a good candidate for more flexible quantities.\n- Supplier 2 (bakery): fixed daily delivery, but they can adjust volumes with 24 hours notice.\n- Supplier 3 (fruit): offers both whole and pre-cut, with some flexibility on product mix.\n\nFor T5, I recommend we prioritize:\n- Supplier 1 and Supplier 3 for flexible quantities and product mix\n- Supplier 2 as a secondary focus for adjusting bakery volumes\n\nOn the operational side, I agree with testing the bakery and fruit changes first in Riverside Grill, as suggested, and starting with greens adjustments in City Center Bistro where storage is less of an issue.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "A3",
            "T4",
            "T5"

          "decision_refs": [],

          "text": "Thanks for the detailed work.\n\nTo keep things safe during the pilot, I propose we:\n- apply the full set of purchasing changes (greens, bakery, pre-cut fruit) only in Riverside Grill for the first two weeks\n- apply only the greens adjustments in City Center Bistro at first\n- keep Airport Express on current rules until we see the first results\n\nThis way, we can monitor A1 and avoid surprises in the most time-sensitive unit.\n\nIf we agree, we can treat these as the revised purchasing rules for the pilot units under T4, documented in A3.",

          "text": "I have shared the draft environmental and biological risk assessment in A5, based on the baseline work in T5.\n\nKey preliminary findings:\n- External environment: low to moderate risk of airborne contaminants from nearby traffic, higher during peak hours.\n- Water: initial samples are within expected ranges, but we should maintain regular monitoring.\n- Internal environment: potential hotspots around waste handling, drains, and high-traffic corridors.\n\nI have also outlined proposed mitigations and monitoring points that will feed into T10 and the SOP pack in A6.\n\nI need your input on:\n1) Which monitoring points and frequencies we should adopt for go-live.\n2) Any design or procedural changes we should implement now, while construction and layout (A3) are still flexible.\n\nPlease review A5 and comment so we can converge on a practical, robust set of controls.",

* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.

          "msg_id": "M11",
          "speaker_id": 87286,
          "reply_to": "M10",
          "text": "Good point. We need to balance detail with something guards can actually keep up with.\nProposal for incidents that must always be logged in the new checklist (A3) once we build it under T4:\n1) Any use of force, restraint, or serious verbal threat.\n2) Any medical event where first aid is given or ambulance is called.\n3) Any fire alarm, smoke detection, or evacuation, including false alarms.\n4) Any confirmed or attempted unauthorized access, tailgating, or badge misuse.\n5) Any suspicion or discovery of illegal substances, weapons, or other prohibited items.\n6) Any involvement of external emergency services.\n7) Any major system failure affecting access control, alarms, or cameras.\n8) Suspicious or damaged packages that require isolation or refusal.\nEverything else can be logged at the guard discretion but these are mandatory.\nIf no one objects, we can treat this as our base list.",
          "artifact_refs": [

It covers what we usually discuss in debriefs and what management asks about.\nFor the scope of phase one zones, I support the four groups you listed earlier. That gives us a mix of public-facing, parking, and industrial risk without stretching shifts too thin.",

The list is clear and we can train new guards on it easily.\nOn the zones, I confirm: hospital-like entrance, commercial main entrance and event hall front, parking areas, and industrial loading dock 1 plus back delivery gate as phase one.\nWe can still note issues in other areas during T1 but focus our first procedures there.",

          "speaker_id": 87286,
          "reply_to": "M13",
          "text": "Thanks all, summarizing so we can move on to the next threads:\nPhase one priority zones:\n1) Hospital-like entrance and lobby.\n2) Commercial main entrance and event hall front.\n3) Parking areas with focus on night.\n4) Industrial loading dock 1 and back delivery gate.\nMandatory incidents to log in the new checklist:\n- Use of force or restraint.\n- Medical events with first aid or ambulance.\n- Any fire alarm or evacuation.\n- Unauthorized access, tailgating, badge misuse.\n- Illegal substances, weapons, or prohibited items.\n- Any involvement of external emergency services.\n- Major system failures affecting access, alarms, or cameras.\n- Suspicious or damaged packages that need isolation or refusal.\nWe will reflect this in A1 and later in A3 when we build the checklist under T4.",
