          "speaker_id": 331660,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "From an admin point of view, A3 and A7 look like they can fit on one page each, which is good.\nWe also need to think about T12: validating that the new process meets safety and hygiene requirements.\nFor that, the health and safety officer will want to see:\n- That A3 is used consistently for at least a week.\n- That A7 is filled in for relevant incidents.\nSo we should be clear in this thread about when exactly staff must use A3 and A7 during the pilot.",

          "speaker_id": 37492,
          "reply_to": "M37",
          "text": "On near-misses: I suggest we do log them in A7, but maybe with a simple tag so we can filter later.\nThat way, we can see patterns without making the form too heavy.\nI will add a field in A7 for 'incident' vs 'near-miss'.\nOn dangerous goods, I will simplify the wording in A3 for this aisle to focus on not stacking cleaning products above food, as you suggest.",

          "speaker_id": 37492,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "For your questions:\n- Yes, we should add a short hand hygiene reminder in A3, especially before handling any open or damaged packaging.\n- For out-of-date items, I propose we log them in A7 only when we find more than a small number at once, for example more than three of the same product or a full case.\nSingle items can just be removed and handled as usual.\nI will update A3 and A7 accordingly.",

          "reply_to": "M42",
          "text": "Thanks, that clarifies it.\nI like the idea of logging only bigger groups of out-of-date items in A7.\nFor A3, grouping checks by role as 300804 suggested would help me quickly see what I need to do at the start of the shift.\nMaybe we can have a small tick box for 'start of shift' and 'end of shift' checks for shelf fillers.",

            "A3",
            "A7",
            "T3",
            "T9",
            "T12"

          "decision_refs": [],

          "speaker_id": 321832,

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

          "text": "Sharing the first draft of the preventive maintenance schedule for PL-01 for review.\nI built it based on the outputs from T1 and the current production calendar in A7, and structured it to feed into T3 and T5.\nKey points:\n- Daily checks: belts, guards, basic lubrication points, visual leaks\n- Weekly checks: sensors cleaning, chain tension, safety interlocks test\n- Monthly checks: deeper inspections on bearings, pneumatics, and electrical panels\nI also drafted a Preventive Maintenance Checklist in line with A2, and cross-checked with A8 to avoid any conflict with environmental and waste handling rules.\nBefore we approve anything (D3, D4), I need your feedback on feasibility during planned downtimes and whether the checklist format works for the team.",

          "text": "On the daily checks, I agree with 11000 that we should keep them tight.\nFrom what I see on PL-01, we can realistically cover lubrication of key points, quick visual checks for leaks, and a fast guard inspection during the pre-start window.\nFor monthly checks, A7 shows a longer planned stop every four weeks; we can use that for the deeper inspections.\nRegarding A8 and T11, I reviewed the waste handling steps in the checklist to ensure we do not create extra risk when draining or disposing of product during maintenance.",

          "text": "From the operator side, the checklist format in A2 is readable, but it would help if we had a very short daily version that can be done at the line, and a more detailed weekly/monthly version for planned stops.\nIf we align the daily checks with the SOP in A3 later, it will be easier for shifts to remember.\nFor timing, if we keep daily checks under 10 minutes, it should fit into the current routine without delaying start-up.\nI do not see any conflict with hygiene rules, but quality should still review the final version for T11.",

          "speaker_id": 386277,

          "text": "Good points.\nI can adjust the draft so that:\n- Daily checks focus on lubrication of critical points, quick guard and leak checks, and basic sensor cleanliness\n- Weekly checks include the more detailed guard fastener checks and full sensor cleaning\nThis should keep daily work within the 10-minute window that 95118 mentioned.\nOn A8 and T11, I checked that any waste generated during cleaning or draining is captured in the existing waste handling steps and that we do not bypass any containment or segregation rules.\nWe will still ask quality and health and safety to sign off before we close D3 and D4.",

          "speaker_id": 95118,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I am sharing the draft SOP for PL-01 start-up, changeover, shutdown, and cleaning, plus a draft operator quick guide for quality and waste checks.\nThe SOP draft is in A3 and is based on inputs from operators on shifts A, B, and C under T4.\nThe quick guide is in A5 and supports T8 and T9.\nKey points in the SOP:\n- Clear sequence for pre-start checks, including the daily maintenance items from A2\n- Standard steps for changeover to minimise product damage and waste\n- Shutdown and cleaning steps aligned with hygiene rules and GMP\nFor the quick guide, I focused on simple visual checks for raw materials, packaging, and main waste points.\nBefore we move to approval (D5, D6), I need feedback on clarity and whether anything is missing for your shifts.",

          "text": "I went through the SOP in A3.\nThe start-up section is clear, but I noticed that the step for checking the flow-wrap film tension is only mentioned under troubleshooting.\nOn the line, we usually adjust film tension before the first run to avoid product damage.\nMaybe we should add that as a standard step in the start-up sequence.\nOn the quick guide in A5, the pictures for acceptable vs non-acceptable packaging look helpful, but we might need one more example for damaged film rolls.",

          "text": "From a maintenance perspective, I like that the SOP start-up section references the daily checks from A2.\nOne thing to consider is adding a short note on what to do if an operator finds an issue during those checks, so they know when to call maintenance vs when they can correct it themselves.\nFor the shutdown and cleaning steps, we should double-check with quality that the sequence matches their expectations, especially around avoiding cross-contamination.\nThis will be important before we confirm D5 and D6.",

          "text": "Overall, the structure of A3 and A5 looks solid.\nTo move toward D5 and D6, I suggest we:\n- Integrate the agreed daily maintenance checks from A2 into the start-up section as a mandatory step\n- Add clear escalation rules for when operators should call maintenance\n- Ensure the quick guide in A5 references both A1 for logging and the new SOP for actions\nOnce we have those tweaks and quality approval, we can confirm D5 (SOP approval) and D6 (final quick guide version).",

          "speaker_id": 95118,

          "text": "Thanks for the feedback.\nI will update A3 to:\n- Add film tension adjustment as a standard start-up step\n- Include a short decision tree for when to call maintenance vs correct locally\n- Highlight guide and sensor adjustments in the changeover section\nFor A5, I will add examples of damaged film rolls and a small box explaining what to log in A1 when we see repeated issues.\nI will then send both A3 and A5 to quality for review under T4, T8, and T9.",

          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 386277,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I am sharing preliminary findings from the root cause analysis on the top recurring mechanical faults for PL-01 under T6.\nThe draft report is in A4.\nBased on the last 3 months of data from T1 and operator feedback, the top 3 faults are:\n1) Film tracking issues causing jams and stoppages\n2) Product misalignment leading to sealing defects and waste\n3) Intermittent sensor failures causing false stops\nFor each, A4 lists suspected root causes and contributing factors.\nI would like your input on which corrective actions we should prioritise within our timebox (D7), and how we can safely pilot any setting changes under T7.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T1",
            "T6",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            33287,
            11000,
            533175,
            95118
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 33287,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "Looking at A4, all three faults are important, but we probably cannot fully address everything within the current project window.\nMy first thought is to prioritise actions that both reduce downtime and cut waste.\nFilm tracking and product misalignment seem to have the biggest combined impact.\nFor T7, we need to define safe parameter ranges with quality before we touch any settings.\nI suggest we focus on:\n- Mechanical adjustments and guides for film tracking\n- Standardised set-up for product alignment\nand treat sensor issues mainly with better checks and replacements for now.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T6",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            386277
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M40",
          "speaker_id": 11000,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "From what I see on the line, film tracking issues cause a lot of short stops and rework.\nOften we adjust the film manually, but it does not always hold.\nIf we can improve the guides or tension settings under T7, that would help.\nFor product misalignment, sometimes it is linked to how we load the infeed, so maybe part of the fix is in the SOP as well as mechanical changes.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T6",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            386277,
            95118
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M41",
          "speaker_id": 533175,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "I agree that film tracking and product misalignment should be our main focus.\nFor sensor failures, many of the issues in A4 look like they can be reduced by better cleaning and positioning, which we already covered in the preventive maintenance checklist.\nSo for D7, I would propose we prioritise:\n1) Film tracking corrective actions\n2) Product alignment and infeed set-up\nand treat sensor improvements as a secondary action that we continue through the new maintenance routines.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A2",
            "T5",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            386277,
            33287
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M42",
          "speaker_id": 95118,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "From the operator logs in A1 and our daily experience, I can confirm that film tracking and misalignment are the most painful.\nThey create both downtime and a lot of waste when packs are not sealed correctly.\nIf we can stabilise those two, it will make a big difference.\nFor sensors, the new cleaning checks in A2 already help, so I am ok with treating that as a follow-on improvement rather than a main focus for D7.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A4",
            "T6",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            386277
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M43",
          "speaker_id": 386277,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "Based on your feedback, I suggest the following for D7:\n- Priority 1: Implement corrective actions on film tracking (guides, rollers, and tension settings) under T7\n- Priority 2: Implement corrective actions on product alignment and infeed set-up, including any SOP tweaks\n- Priority 3: Continue sensor improvements mainly through the new maintenance and cleaning routines\nFor T7, I will work with quality to define safe parameter ranges before we run any pilots.\nDoes anyone see a reason to change this order?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T6",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            33287,
            11000,
            533175,
            95118
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M44",
          "speaker_id": 33287,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "I support that prioritisation.\nIt matches the impact we see in A4 and what the team is reporting.\nFor T7, we should also make sure we log the before and after waste and downtime in A6 so we can show the effect of the changes.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A6",
            "T7",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            386277

          "speaker_id": 11000,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "The order works for me.\nWhen we pilot the new film tracking settings, I can be on the line to help monitor how stable they are and note any side effects.\nWe should also brief operators on what to watch for during the pilot so they can give feedback quickly.",

          "text": "From a supervision point of view, if we do not tackle bay allocation and parts waiting, the lane will still feel blocked even if the handover is better.\nMy suggestion for D2 later would be:\n1) Improve sales-to-workshop handover quality.\n2) Introduce a structured intake and triage check in the lane.\n3) Define basic bay allocation and prioritisation rules.\nCustomer communication will improve as a result of the first two, but we can also add a simple script without making it a separate top pain point.\nOpen to adjusting this if others see it differently.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            535963,
            21331,
            247886
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M10",
          "speaker_id": 20895,
          "reply_to": "M9",
          "text": "I like that list.\nFrom the lane, the structured intake and triage check will help us a lot with safety and quick diagnostics. If we combine that with better handover information, we will spend less time chasing details.\nFor bay allocation, even a simple rule like urgent and warranty first, then routine, would already be a big step.\nSo I support those three as the main focus for D2.",

            "A1"

          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            118321

        },
        {

          "speaker_id": 535963,
          "reply_to": "M7",
          "text": "I have now updated A1 with the extra branches and steps we discussed:\n- Separate entry points for sales-led bookings and direct service visits.\n- Explicit quick safety and visual check in the lane.\n- Informal callbacks to customers when information is missing.\n- Note about cars waiting in bays for parts.\nUnless anyone spots a major gap, I suggest we treat this as the final current-state map for T1 and move on to designing the future flow.\nPlease shout if there is any missing step that would change how we design the pilot.",

          "speaker_id": 247886,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "I checked the updated A1 and from what I see on the ground it matches our current reality.\nThe only thing I will keep an eye on is how often customers bypass the front desk, but that is already shown as a branch.\nFrom my side, we can close T1 on the mapping part.",

          "speaker_id": 21331,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "I have also reviewed A1 focusing on the sales and booking steps.\nThe two paths you added (sale plus future service, and direct service) look right to me. The double entry of data is visible, which is good for later.\nI am comfortable using this as our baseline map for the project.",

        {

          "speaker_id": 118321,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "From the supervision and bay allocation side, the updated A1 reflects how we currently assign work and where we get blocked.\nI agree with closing the current-state mapping and moving on to the design tasks T2, T3, and T4.\nOn the pain point priorities for D2, I still support the three I listed earlier unless someone wants to swap one out.",

        {

          "speaker_id": 535963,
          "reply_to": "M14",
          "text": "Let us close D2 so we can brief the design work clearly.\nBased on the discussion, I propose the top three pain points we will address in the pilot design are:\n1) Incomplete or low-quality sales-to-workshop handover information.\n2) Lack of a structured intake and triage check in the lane.\n3) No clear bay allocation and prioritisation rules, leading to blocked capacity.\nCustomer communication at intake will be improved as part of the first two.\nIf there are no objections, we will use these three to guide T2, T3, and T4.",

          "msg_id": "M19",
          "speaker_id": 21331,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "As agreed in TH1, I have drafted the new sales-to-workshop handover form and intake script and added them into A2, linked to T2.\nStructure of the form:\n- Customer and vehicle details (to avoid double entry later).\n- Reason for visit, with guided questions for symptoms (warning lights, noises, when it happens, previous work).\n- Customer expectations (wait, leave car, preferred contact, budget indication).\n- Safety notes and visible damage.\nThe script mirrors the form so that we can follow it in person or on the phone.\nSharing here for feedback, especially from the workshop and supervision side, before we lock the mandatory fields for D3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            247886,
            20895,
            118321,
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M20",
          "speaker_id": 247886,
          "reply_to": "M19",
          "text": "I went through A2 with a workshop lens.\nPositive points:\n- The symptom questions will really help for electrical and intermittent issues.\n- Capturing previous work on the same problem is important for warranty.\nSuggestions:\n- Add a field for dashboard warning lights with options (engine, ABS, airbag, etc.).\n- Include a checkbox for whether the customer has left any personal items in the car, to avoid disputes.\nFor D3, I would consider the following as mandatory fields: vehicle identification, main complaint description, symptom details, previous related work, and customer contact preference.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            21331
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M21",
          "speaker_id": 20895,
          "reply_to": "M19",
          "text": "From my side, A2 already covers most of what I usually have to ask again at the lane.\nOne more detail that would help the triage checklist later: a simple field for whether the issue is safety-critical from the customer point of view (for example, brakes, steering, tyres). Even if their judgement is not perfect, it helps us prioritise.\nAlso, could we add a small section for known modifications or accessories (tow bar, aftermarket electronics)? That often affects diagnostics.\nThese would feed nicely into A3 when we build the intake and triage checklist under T3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            21331,
            247886
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M22",
          "speaker_id": 118321,
          "reply_to": "M19",
          "text": "Looking at A2 from a coordination angle, I like that it already includes customer expectations and preferred contact.\nTo connect with T4 later, I suggest we add a simple job type classification on the form: urgent safety, warranty, routine service, diagnostic only, accessories.\nThis will allow us to apply bay allocation rules more easily.\nFor D3, I would make job type classification mandatory as well, otherwise the triage in the lane will still be guesswork.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            21331,
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M23",
          "speaker_id": 535963,
          "reply_to": "M19",
          "text": "Thanks for the draft, this is a good step.\nFrom a customer and operations view, I want to keep the form usable at the front desk and on the sales floor.\nTwo checks:\n- Can we keep the number of mandatory fields limited so that intake time stays under the 20-minute target?\n- Are all fields compatible with our existing system, or do we need a paper add-on for some items?\nFor D3, I would like us to agree on a core set of mandatory fields that we can realistically capture every time, and mark the rest as recommended.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            21331
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M24",
          "speaker_id": 21331,
          "reply_to": "M23",
          "text": "Good point on intake time.\nI checked against our current system screens. Most of the customer and vehicle fields already exist. The new parts are mainly the symptom guidance, safety-critical flag, job type classification, and personal items note.\nProposal for D3 mandatory fields:\n- Customer and vehicle identification.\n- Main complaint description.\n- Symptom details (structured questions).\n- Job type classification.\n- Customer contact preference.\nThe rest (previous work, modifications, personal items, safety-critical flag) can be recommended but not strictly mandatory.\nIf we agree, I will update A2 accordingly.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            535963,
            247886,
            20895,
            118321
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M25",
          "speaker_id": 247886,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "I can work with that list.\nEven if previous work and safety-critical flag are not mandatory, we can emphasise them in training so they are used most of the time.\nFrom the lane side, as long as we always get the main complaint, symptom details, and job type, we can build a solid triage in A3.\nSo I support your proposal for D3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            21331
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 20895,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "Agreed from my side as well.\nThose mandatory fields will already reduce a lot of back-and-forth.\nWhen we design the triage checklist under T3, we can reference these fields directly so technicians know where to look on the form.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            21331
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 118321,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "I am fine with that mandatory set.\nJob type classification being mandatory is the key link to T4 and later to A5.\nLet us lock D3 with that structure so we can move on to the triage checklist and the new lane workflow.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T4",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            21331,
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 21331,
          "reply_to": "M27",
          "text": "Understood, I will update A2 with the agreed mandatory and recommended fields and mark T2 as ready for validation.\nSwitching to the triage checklist: @247886 shared a first draft of A3 linked to T3.\nCould you summarise the main steps here so we can review and then close D4 on the triage flow?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "T2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            247886
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 247886,
          "reply_to": "M28",
          "text": "Sure, here is the structure of the triage checklist in A3 for T3:\n1) Safety and basic checks in the lane: leaks, tyre condition, lights, warning messages, obvious damage, personal items.\n2) Confirm complaint and symptom details with the customer or from A2, correcting anything unclear.\n3) Quick functional checks based on job type (for example, brake pedal feel for brake jobs, battery test for electrical complaints).\n4) Documentation: record findings, note any extra work suggested, and confirm with customer before proceeding.\n5) Bay assignment suggestion based on job type and estimated time, to feed into T4 and A5.\nTiming-wise, the goal is to keep this triage under 10 minutes per vehicle so we stay within the 20-minute intake target overall.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A2",
            "T3",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            21331,
            118321
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M30",
          "speaker_id": 20895,
          "reply_to": "M29",
          "text": "I like the structure.\nOne practical suggestion: in step 3, maybe we can group the quick checks into a short list per job type so technicians do not have to think from scratch each time.\nFor example, for routine service: fluid levels, visible leaks, tyre wear, lights. For electrical: battery test, check fuses, scan for codes if available.\nThat will help keep the triage within the 10-minute target.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            247886
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M31",
          "speaker_id": 118321,
          "reply_to": "M29",
          "text": "From a coordination point of view, I want to make sure the triage output is clear enough for bay allocation.\nCould we add a simple triage outcome field at the end of A3: ready for bay, needs parts check first, needs customer decision, or safety do not move?\nThis will connect directly into the lane workflow and A5 under T4.\nIf we include that, I am comfortable approving the steps and timing for D4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A5",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            247886,
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M32",
          "speaker_id": 247886,
          "reply_to": "M31",
          "text": "Good idea.\nI will add that triage outcome field to A3 and also group the quick checks by job type as @20895 suggested.\nWith those adjustments, the checklist will still fit on one page and should be practical to use in the lane.\nFrom my side, the steps and timing are ready to be approved for D4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            118321,
            20895
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M33",
          "speaker_id": 535963,
          "reply_to": "M32",
          "text": "Let us close D4.\nWe will adopt the triage checklist in A3 with the following structure:\n- Safety and basic checks in the lane.\n- Confirmation of complaint and symptom details using A2.\n- Short, job-type-based quick checks.\n- Documentation of findings and customer confirmation.\n- Triage outcome (ready for bay, parts check first, customer decision, safety do not move).\nTarget triage time is under 10 minutes per vehicle.\nThis will feed into the new lane workflow and bay allocation rules in T4 and A5.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A2",
            "T3",
            "T4",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D4"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            247886,
            20895,
            118321,
            21331
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M34",
          "speaker_id": 21331,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "All clear from my side.\nI will align the intake script in A2 with the triage steps in A3 so that the questions flow naturally from sales or front desk to the lane.\nWith D3 and D4 closed, T2 and T3 are ready for training preparation later.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          "msg_id": "M35",
          "speaker_id": 535963,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have drafted the lane capacity rules and the staff rota for the pilot and added them into A5 and A8, linked to T5 and T8.\nKey points:\n- Pilot proposal: start in two weeks, run for 10 working days.\n- Lane capacity: target of 4 intake slots per hour, with a maximum of 2 triage cases in progress at the same time.\n- Bay allocation rules in A5: urgent safety and warranty first, then routine service, then diagnostics and accessories.\n- Rota in A8: one dedicated intake technician per shift, one backup technician during peaks, and clear time blocks for sellers to handle intake using A2.\nPlease review and comment, especially on whether the capacity assumptions are realistic and if the rota covers peak times properly, before we close D5 and D6.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A8",
            "T5",
            "T8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            118321,
            247886,
            20895,
            21331
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 118321,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "I checked A5 and A8.\nOn capacity: 4 intake slots per hour with triage under 10 minutes seems achievable if we avoid long conversations at the front.\nOn rota: the dedicated intake technician per shift is good, but I notice that on late afternoons we only have the backup technician for one hour. That is usually when customers rush in after work.\nSuggestion: extend the backup technician coverage by one more hour in the afternoon, even if that means slightly less time on other tasks.\nFor D5, I am comfortable with the proposed start in two weeks and 10 working days duration, as long as we confirm training dates for T6 and T7 beforehand.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A8",
            "T5",
            "T7",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M37",
          "speaker_id": 247886,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "From the lane side, the capacity numbers look tight but manageable if we stick to the triage checklist in A3.\nI agree with @118321 that late afternoon is a risk. That is when we see more walk-ins and people wanting to wait.\nCould we also define an overflow rule in A5: if more than 2 triage cases are waiting, we temporarily redirect routine jobs to standard bays without full triage, just basic safety checks?\nThat would help avoid long queues in the lane.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            535963,
            118321
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 20895,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "Looking at A8, I see I am scheduled as intake technician on three mornings and two afternoons during the pilot.\nThat is fine for me, but we should make sure there is time blocked for cleaning the lane and checking safety items, not only triage.\nMaybe we can add a short daily slot in the rota for lane housekeeping so it does not get forgotten.\nOn the pilot start date, two weeks from now gives us enough time to get used to A2 and A3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "A3",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 21331,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "From the sales side, A8 shows two sellers covering intake blocks in the morning and one in the afternoon.\nAfternoons are usually busier for test drives and new sales, so I am a bit concerned about having only one seller available for intake then.\nCould we shift one of the morning intake blocks to the afternoon, or at least have a flexible slot that we can move based on bookings?\nFor D5, I am ok with the pilot start in two weeks, but I will need to plan T6 training sessions next week to avoid clashes with peak sales times.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M40",
          "speaker_id": 535963,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "Good feedback.\nI will adjust A8 to:\n- Extend backup technician coverage by one extra hour in the late afternoon.\n- Move one seller intake block from morning to afternoon, and mark one additional block as flexible depending on bookings.\n- Add a 15-minute lane housekeeping slot at the start of each shift for the intake technician.\nOn overflow, I like @247886 suggestion. I will add to A5 that if more than 2 triage cases are waiting, routine jobs can be sent to standard bays with only basic safety checks.\nWith these changes, are we comfortable confirming D5: pilot start in two weeks, duration 10 working days?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A8",
            "T5",
            "T8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            118321,
            247886,
            20895,
            21331
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M41",
          "speaker_id": 118321,
          "reply_to": "M40",
          "text": "With those rota and rule adjustments in A5 and A8, I am comfortable confirming D5.\nTwo weeks gives us time to complete T6 and T7 and to brief the team on the overflow rule.\nI will also prepare a short visual of the bay allocation logic from A5 to post in the workshop.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "A8",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D5"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M42",
          "speaker_id": 247886,
          "reply_to": "M40",
          "text": "Agreed on D5 from my side.\nThe overflow rule in A5 will be important to explain clearly to technicians so they know when to skip full triage.\nI can help during T7 training to walk through a few examples.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D5"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            535963,
            118321
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M43",
          "speaker_id": 21331,
          "reply_to": "M40",
          "text": "I am ok with the pilot start and duration.\nThe updated A8 with more afternoon coverage should balance sales and intake better.\nI will schedule T6 sessions for the sales team next week so everyone is ready before go-live.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D5"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M44",
          "speaker_id": 20895,
          "reply_to": "M40",
          "text": "From the lane, the adjusted rota in A8 looks workable.\nThe housekeeping slot will help keep the area safe and organised.\nI am aligned with D5 and ready to support during the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D5"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            535963
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M45",

A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

          "text": "On late shift we often find open containers of degreaser left on benches. In A2 I suggest we add a rule that all chemical containers must be closed and returned to the chemical zone immediately after use, no exceptions. For A6, we can mark that zone clearly on the floor and on shelves so it is obvious where things go.",

          "speaker_id": 203126,

          "text": "For PPE, could A2 include a simple table: for each common substance (engine oil, hydraulic oil, brake cleaner, degreaser, battery acid), list required gloves, eye protection, and any extra like apron? That would make it easier for new staff to follow without reading long text.",
          "artifact_refs": [

        {
          "msg_id": "M42",
          "speaker_id": 38857,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "Sometimes I am not sure where to put used rags soaked with oil or cleaner. Can we include in A2 and A6 a clear rule and a labelled bin for oily rags so they do not end up in general waste?",

            108987

        {

          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "For spill response, I suggest A2 defines three simple steps: 1) stop the source if safe; 2) contain with absorbent from the spill kit; 3) dispose of used absorbent in the correct waste container.             "T3"

          "mentions": [
            108987
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M44",
          "speaker_id": 156061,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "Agree. We should also define in A6 that spill kits have a fixed location and are checked at least weekly, maybe as part of the deep-check routine in T2 or the cleaning standard in T9. Empty kits are a common problem.",

        {

          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "On workshop organisation, I propose in A6 we define three zones: tools, chemicals, and waste.         {
          "msg_id": "M46",
          "speaker_id": 38857,
          "reply_to": "M45",
          "text": "For the end-of-shift cleaning in T9, could we keep it to a short list so it is realistic? Maybe: clear floors of tools and parts, wipe up any spills, return tools to boards, empty small waste bins if full, and check that chemical containers are closed.",

          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M46",
          "text": "That sounds reasonable. We can put those steps into A6 as the standard and link them to T9. For hazardous substances in A2, we should also mention that decanting into unlabelled bottles is not allowed. All containers must have the original label or a clear secondary label.",

          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Yesterday we had a minor incident: during a check, I found a loose hydraulic hose on one of the rear-loaders. No spill, but it could have failed on the road. I tightened it and noted it in my notebook, but I was not sure how to log it properly or how clearly to mark the truck as not to be used until checked. With T5 and A4 in mind, how do we want to record this kind of near-miss and how should we flag a 'do not use' vehicle as part of T11?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987,
            109283,
            38857,
            156061
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M56",
          "speaker_id": 108987,
          "reply_to": "M55",
          "text": "Good example. For A4, I propose we always log near-misses like that, even if we fix them on the spot. Fields could be: date and time, vehicle ID, location (yard, workshop, on route), type (incident or near-miss), short description, immediate action taken, and who was informed. That would meet T5 and help us spot patterns.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M57",
          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M55",
          "text": "On the 'do not use' side for T11, I suggest we define clear criteria: any safety-critical defect (brakes, steering, major fluid leak, loose wheel nuts, serious hydraulic issue) means the vehicle must not leave the yard until repaired or cleared by a supervisor. For your hose case, if there was any doubt about the fix, it should have been marked as not to be used.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126,
            108987
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M58",
          "speaker_id": 38857,
          "reply_to": "M55",
          "text": "Sometimes I am not sure if something is safety-critical or not. Could A4 or the T11 process include a short list of examples, like brake warning light on, big oil leak, steering play, so we know when to definitely mark 'do not use'?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            109283
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M59",
          "speaker_id": 156061,
          "reply_to": "M58",
          "text": "We can add a simple reference list to the T11 procedure and post it near the board. For the visual method, I suggest we use a bright red magnetic tag on the board layout in A3 and a matching red tag on the vehicle key. If the tag is on, the vehicle is not to be used.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987,
            109283
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M60",
          "speaker_id": 108987,
          "reply_to": "M59",
          "text": "I like the red tag idea. For T11 we can define the steps: 1) mark the vehicle as 'do not use' on the board in A3 with a red magnet; 2) attach a red tag to the key; 3) write a short note on the board with the reason; 4) log the issue in A4 if it is an incident or near-miss; 5) inform the fleet supervisor.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A4",
            "T11",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            156061
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M61",
          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": "M56",
          "text": "For A4, do we want a free text description only, or also a simple category like mechanical, electrical, bodywork, slip or trip, chemical spill? Categories might help when we review logs later.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987,
            109283
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M62",
          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M61",
          "text": "Good idea. We can add a simple category field to A4 with a short list as you suggested. That will still keep T5 simple but make the weekly review easier when we get to T12.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M63",
          "speaker_id": 38857,
          "reply_to": "M60",
          "text": "If a vehicle is marked 'do not use' with the red tag, who is allowed to remove the tag once it is fixed? I want to avoid someone just taking it off without checking properly.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M64",
          "speaker_id": 156061,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "We should say in T11 that only the fleet supervisor or a designated senior attendant can remove the red tag and clear the vehicle on A3, after confirming the repair. That keeps the decision with someone accountable.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            38857,
            108987
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M65",
          "speaker_id": 108987,
          "reply_to": "M64",
          "text": "Agree. I will check with the fleet supervisor, but the default in T11 can be that they or their delegate remove the tag. For us, the rule is simple: if the red tag is on the board or key, the vehicle does not leave the yard.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T11",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            156061
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M66",
          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": "M56",
          "text": "Back to A4, should we log very small things like a missing mirror cap, or only items that could have caused harm or damage? I do not want the log to become so full that people stop reading it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            109283,
            108987
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M67",
          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M66",
          "text": "I would say A4 is for anything that had or could have had safety, environmental, or major operational impact. Cosmetic issues like small scratches can stay in normal maintenance notes. We can add that guidance into T5 so people know what belongs in the log.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M68",
          "speaker_id": 38857,
          "reply_to": "M55",
          "text": "For my hose example, based on what we said, I should have: marked the truck as 'do not use' with a red tag, logged it in A4 as a near-miss with category mechanical, and told the supervisor. That helps me understand the new process.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T11",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            203126
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M69",
          "speaker_id": 108987,
          "reply_to": "M67",
          "text": "To summarise: for A4 and T5 we will use fields date and time, vehicle ID, location, type (incident or near-miss), category, description, immediate action, and who was informed. For T11 we will use red tags on the board in A3 and on keys, with clear criteria for when to apply them and only the supervisor or delegate allowed to remove them. Is everyone ok with that as our standard?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5",
            "T11",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            109283,
            203126,
            38857,
            156061
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M70",
          "speaker_id": 203126,
          "reply_to": "M69",
          "text": "Yes, that works for me. It is clear enough to follow even when it is busy.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            108987
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M71",
          "speaker_id": 109283,
          "reply_to": "M69",
          "text": "I am aligned as well. The combination of A4 and the red tag process in T11 should make it much harder for serious issues to slip through.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [

        {

            108987
          ]
        },
        {

          "speaker_id": 108987,
          "reply_to": "M72",

        {
          "msg_id": "M74",
          "speaker_id": 109283,

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

          "text": "As promised, here is the first draft outline for the survey templates (A5, T5) and the continuous improvement process (T12), plus a proposal for the monthly reporting template (A8, T9).\n1) Survey templates (A5, T5)\n- Employee survey (quarterly):\n  - awareness of wellbeing guidelines (A1)\n  - perceived usefulness of wellbeing activities\n  - experience with hybrid routines (on-site and remote)\n  - open question for suggestions.\n- Client survey (per visit, then summarised quarterly):\n  - overall satisfaction with the visit\n  - perception of the office environment and wellbeing aspects\n  - clarity of agenda and logistics (A2, A3)\n  - likelihood to recommend visiting again.\n2) Continuous improvement process (T12)\n- Data sources: surveys (A5), monthly status reports (A8), ad-hoc feedback.\n- Roles:\n  - I consolidate wellbeing-related feedback\n  - sales consolidates client-related feedback\n  - assistants flag operational issues.\n- Cadence: monthly quick review, quarterly deeper review.\n3) Monthly reporting template (A8, T9)\n- Sections:\n  - key activities (visits and wellbeing sessions)\n  - attendance and basic metrics\n  - issues and risks\n  - improvement actions decided.\nPlease review the structure and suggest changes before we finalise the questions and format.",

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.

ROLE INSTRUCTIONS
You are an EVALUATOR that infers latent behavioral signals from Slack-style corporate conversations.
You do NOT have access to the true scenario labels. You must infer using ONLY:
* trajectory_signature / the participant’s trajectory and summarized history (to calibrate vocabulary and context);
* the channel content and structure (messages + artifact_refs + decision_refs + thread_outcome).

CRITICAL OUTPUT RESTRICTIONS
* Return ONLY a single valid JSON object in the schema specified at the end.
* Do not include text outside the JSON.
* Do not use numbers (no score, no probability, no confidence).
* For each attribute, return ONLY one label in {LOW, MID, HIGH}.
* DETERMINISTIC RULE: if you are unsure/ambiguous, choose MID.
* Evidence snippets must be SHORT QUOTES from the text (no comments) and must NOT contain “LOW/MID/HIGH”.
* DO NOT use literal line breaks inside strings. If needed, use \n or if it is a tab use \t.
* Ensure quotes and braces are closed.

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

INPUT
* participants_json: list of participants, each with:
    {
        "_id": int,
        "role": string,                            # role of the participant

        "trajectory_summary": string,              # consolidated summary (may contain “->”)

    }
* channel: threads and messages (msg_id, speaker_id, reply_to, text, mentions, artifact_refs, decision_refs, reactions)
* (optional) thread_outcome per thread (decisions_made, next_steps)

IMPORTANT: You will use the participants' information [INPUT PARTICIPANTS] as a basis to try to infer the skill, productivity, and performance levels of each participant. Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:
   * Messages where speaker_id == the participant’s _id.
   * If the participant speaks little, you can also use messages that mention them (mentions contains _id) as contextual evidence.
2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of HIGH => candidate HIGH
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of LOW  => candidate LOW
   * otherwise => MID
3. Attention:

   * In the corporate context, everyone needs to deliver and demonstrate work; be careful to infer HIGH for something standard that should be MID.
   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:
   * If there are no messages from the participant, use MID for all three attributes and use evidence from a message where they were mentioned.

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.
