HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.

          "speaker_id": 167595,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Sharing the first draft of the job posting and interview toolkit for review.\nThis will become A4 and is linked to T2.\nKey elements:\n- Job posting template with sections for role summary, responsibilities, requirements, and a standard inclusion statement, plus notes on inclusive language.\n- Structured interview guide with core behavioural questions and prompts to explore accommodations where relevant.\n- Simple scorecard with clear criteria to reduce bias.\nI drafted it to align with the early view of A1 so that the steps from requisition to offer are consistent.\nI would like feedback on:\n1) Clarity for non HR managers.\n2) Any legal or employment law red flags.\n3) Anything missing from an inclusion perspective before we move to pilot approval under D3.\nAlso, 17956, I know you are working on T3 and A2; it would be good to check that the toolkit and the guideline use the same concepts.",

          "text": "I checked the interview guide from a practical point of view.\nThe flow is easy to follow, but I wonder if we should add a short section on how to open and close the interview, since some managers are not used to structured interviews.\nAlso, maybe we can add a note reminding them not to ask about family plans or similar topics, which often come up informally.",

          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 167595,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I am sharing the draft onboarding checklist and 90 day integration plan, which will become A3 and is linked to T4.\nStructure:\n- Pre boarding: contracts, equipment, system access, and welcome communication.\n- First week: orientation, manager check ins, basic training, and introductions.\n- First month: role specific training, feedback touchpoint, and inclusion check.\n- 90 days: performance and integration review, plus feedback from the new hire.\nI tried to align the steps with the process map in A1 and kept the checklist simple enough for managers.\nI would like feedback on:\n1) Feasibility from a payroll and HRIS perspective (T5).\n2) Whether we are covering people with disabilities and remote hires clearly enough.\n3) Any steps that feel too heavy for managers.\nOnce we refine this, we can move toward D5 and D6.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T4",
            "A1",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            441030,

        {
          "msg_id": "M37",
          "speaker_id": 441030,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "Thanks for the draft.\nFrom a payroll and HRIS angle, most steps look fine.\nA couple of points for T5:\n- For pre boarding, we should make sure the contract creation and HRIS entry happen before equipment ordering, otherwise we risk delays.\n- For 90 day reviews, we should confirm whether we track this in HRIS or via a simple form, to avoid adding manual follow up.\nIf we keep the checklist aligned with existing fields, D6 should be straightforward.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            167595
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 17956,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "Looking at A3 from a legal and compliance perspective, I do not see major issues.\nWe just need to ensure that any mandatory documents or medical checks required by local labour legislation are captured in the pre boarding section, maybe as a note that can vary by region.\nFor people with disabilities, we might want to add a step to confirm accommodations before day one and to review them during the first month.\nThat would also connect well with the inclusive hiring guideline in A2.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",

          "decision_refs": [],

            167595

        },

          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 549423,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "I checked the checklist with a focus on manager usability.\nThe structure is clear, but I suggest we:\n- Add a short summary at the top with the key actions for each phase.\n- Include a simple reminder for managers to introduce the new hire to any disability support resources we have.\nFor remote hires, maybe we can add a note about virtual introductions and equipment shipping timelines.",

          "msg_id": "M40",
          "speaker_id": 552174,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "From a practical side, I think managers will appreciate checkboxes and short descriptions rather than long text.\nMaybe we can also add a line for a 30 day check in, not only at 90 days, so issues are caught earlier.\nOtherwise, the flow looks manageable.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          "speaker_id": 82204,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "I like the overall structure of A3.\nTo keep it lean and avoid the risk of low adoption, I would:\n- Highlight which steps are mandatory versus recommended.\n- Make sure the pre boarding steps are as automated as possible through HRIS and payroll, in line with T5.\nIf we can confirm with 441030 that the sequence works with current systems, we should be close to D5 and D6.",

          "text": "Thanks for the inputs.\nI will adjust A3 to:\n- Make contract creation and HRIS entry explicit before equipment ordering.\n- Add a note that 90 day reviews can be tracked either in HRIS where available or via a simple form, to avoid blocking rollout.\nI will also incorporate the suggestions on disability accommodations, remote hires, and mandatory versus recommended steps.\nOnce updated, I will share a short summary so we can decide on D5 and D6.",

          "msg_id": "M50",
          "speaker_id": 82204,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Now that A2, A3, and A4 are in good shape, we need to plan the pilot.\nProposal for D7:\n- Pilot business unit: Customer Operations, as they have a steady volume of hiring and a mix of on site and remote roles.\n- Timeframe: next 4 weeks, within our overall 30 day project window.\nScope for the pilot under T8:\n- At least three roles hired using the new process.\n- Use of A1, A2, A3, and A4 end to end.\nFor D8 and T7, we also need to approve the manager communication and training plan.\nInitial idea:\n- Short virtual training session (45 minutes) for Customer Operations managers.\n- Manager Communication and Training Pack (A6) with a quick reference guide and FAQ.\nPlease share any concerns with the proposed business unit and dates, or alternative suggestions, before we lock in D7 and D8.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",

        {
          "msg_id": "M51",
          "speaker_id": 17956,
          "reply_to": "M50",
          "text": "Customer Operations sounds like a good choice for the pilot, since they have enough volume to test the framework properly.\nOnly concern is that they sometimes have urgent hires, so we should be careful that the new process does not slow them down too much.\nMaybe we can agree with their manager on which roles will go through the pilot and which can follow the old process if there is an emergency.\nOn the training, a 45 minute session seems reasonable, as long as the materials in A6 are very clear and not too long.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "T8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],

            82204

        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M52",
          "speaker_id": 441030,
          "reply_to": "M50",
          "text": "I support using Customer Operations for the pilot.\nFrom a payroll and HRIS perspective, they are already used to structured processes, so it should be manageable.\nWe just need to make sure the managers understand that the new steps do not change how they submit data to payroll.\nFor T7, I suggest we include one slide in A6 that shows clearly what stays the same and what changes for them.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          "speaker_id": 167595,
          "reply_to": "M50",
          "text": "I agree that Customer Operations is a good pilot area.\nFor T7, I can draft the training deck and quick reference guide for A6, focusing on:\n- How to use A2, A3, and A4 in practice.\n- What is mandatory versus recommended.\n- How to escalate issues using T11 once it is ready.\nOn timing, if we confirm D7 and D8 this week, we can schedule two training sessions next week to cover different time zones.",

          "speaker_id": 549423,
          "reply_to": "M53",
          "text": "I can help with the FAQ section for A6 under T7.\nBased on past questions from managers, I will include topics like:\n- How to handle candidates who request accommodations.\n- What to do if they are short on time but still need to follow the new steps.\n- Who to contact if they are unsure about a legal or payroll question.\nThis should support both D7 and D8 by making the pilot smoother.",

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

ROLE INSTRUCTIONS
You are an EVALUATOR that infers latent behavioral signals from Slack-style corporate conversations.
You do NOT have access to the true scenario labels. You must infer using ONLY:
* trajectory_signature / the participant’s trajectory and summarized history (to calibrate vocabulary and context);
* the channel content and structure (messages + artifact_refs + decision_refs + thread_outcome).

CRITICAL OUTPUT RESTRICTIONS
* Return ONLY a single valid JSON object in the schema specified at the end.
* Do not include text outside the JSON.
* Do not use numbers (no score, no probability, no confidence).
* For each attribute, return ONLY one label in {LOW, MID, HIGH}.
* DETERMINISTIC RULE: if you are unsure/ambiguous, choose MID.
* Evidence snippets must be SHORT QUOTES from the text (no comments) and must NOT contain “LOW/MID/HIGH”.
* DO NOT use literal line breaks inside strings. If needed, use \n or if it is a tab use \t.
* Ensure quotes and braces are closed.

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

INPUT
* participants_json: list of participants, each with:
    {
        "_id": int,
        "role": string,                            # role of the participant
        "trajectory_lastK": [string],              # ESCO titles (short list, in chronological order)
        "trajectory_summary": string,              # consolidated summary (may contain “->”)
        "skills_text": string,                     # skills extracted from trajectory
    }
* channel: threads and messages (msg_id, speaker_id, reply_to, text, mentions, artifact_refs, decision_refs, reactions)
* (optional) thread_outcome per thread (decisions_made, next_steps)

IMPORTANT: You will use the participants' information [INPUT PARTICIPANTS] as a basis to try to infer the skill, productivity, and performance levels of each participant. Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.

          "speaker_id": 47149,
          "reply_to": "M77",
          "text": "From my shifts, the biggest win was moving morning hygiene clearly before breakfast and meds. A7 shows fewer clashes and fewer cold meals. I think we should definitely keep that.             "A7",
            "A3"

            3328

          "reply_to": "M77",
          "text": "On the childcare side, A7 shows that the emotional check-ins at the start of activities worked well.           "speaker_id": 107378,

          "text": "Highlights from T6 and A5:\n- Payroll folders (digital and physical) are restricted to payroll and finance; HR has access only to HR-specific subfolders.\n- Office can see only the intake log and scanned forms needed for routing, not full payroll reports.\n- Sharing by email must use the minimum necessary data; sensitive attachments go to named recipients only.\n- Retention: payroll reports kept for 10 years, supporting documents for 5 years, in line with our usual practice.\nFrom T11 and A8:\n- Common discrepancy scenarios: missing hours, wrong rate, missing overtime, incorrect bank details.\n- First contact: payroll checks A2 and source documents; if confirmed, we contact office or HR depending on the issue.\n- If not resolved within 2 business days, escalate to the manager; urgent cases affecting current pay are handled same day where possible.\nPlease check if these rules are workable from your side.",

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

          "msg_id": "M21",
          "speaker_id": 6784,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Starting the pricing and margin discussion for the Launch of Unified B2B Service Bundles.\nI have uploaded the first draft of the pricing and margin model in A2, based on the MVP bundles defined in A1.\nThe model covers list prices, standard discounts by segment, and a preliminary margin view, aligned with T3 and the KPI thinking in T10.\nKey points:\n- Target margin range currently sits between 32 percent and 38 percent across bundles.\n- Standard discount bands by segment: up to 10 percent for mid-market, 15 percent for enterprise renewals, 8 percent for digital natives.\nPlease review A2 and share any concerns on the ranges or discount rules before we take this to finance for formal approval.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A1",
            "T3",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],

        {
          "msg_id": "M22",
          "speaker_id": 90589,
          "reply_to": "M21",
          "text": "I went through A2.\nFrom a market and channel perspective, the list prices look broadly in line with what we see from competitors, but the discount band for enterprise renewals might be a bit tight.\nIn practice, sales often needs up to 20 percent to win back accounts at risk.\nCould we define a standard band up to 15 percent, with a controlled exception process up to 20 percent for specific cases, so we do not break the margin guardrails in T3?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            6784
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M23",
          "speaker_id": 82217,
          "reply_to": "M21",
          "text": "Looking at A2 now.\nI see the margin range you mentioned, but I am not fully sure how the discount rules interact with the KPIs in T10.\nIf we allow higher discounts for enterprise renewals, do we still stay above the minimum margin target in the project constraints?\nDo we need a separate guardrail for each bundle, or can we define a single minimum margin across all bundles?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            6784
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M24",
          "speaker_id": 447542,
          "reply_to": "M23",
          "text": "Good point.\nFrom what I see in A2, the sensitivity tab shows that if we go to 20 percent discount on enterprise renewals, some bundles drop close to 30 percent margin.\nGiven the project constraint to maintain or improve current gross margin, I would suggest we set a hard minimum margin per bundle, not just overall.\nMaybe we can agree that no deal should go below 30 percent margin without finance approval.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            6784,
            82217

        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M25",
          "speaker_id": 6784,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "On the enterprise renewals discount band: I like the idea of a standard band plus an exception process.\nIn A2, I can set:\n- Standard discount up to 15 percent for enterprise renewals.\n- Exception band up to 20 percent, but only if the resulting margin stays above a defined minimum.\nWe can then document the approval flow with finance in T3.\nI will also add a note in T10 so that we track the impact of these exceptions on revenue and margin KPIs.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3",
            "T10"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            90589
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 6784,
          "reply_to": "M23",
          "text": "On the margin guardrails: my proposal is to define a target range and a hard floor.\nBased on A2, I suggest:\n- Target margin range: 32 percent to 38 percent for most deals.\n- Hard minimum margin per bundle: 30 percent, below which finance must approve.\nThis way, we respect the project constraint on gross margin while giving sales some flexibility.\nIf we agree, I will reflect this in A2 and in the documentation for T3.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            82217,
            447542
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 83919,
          "reply_to": "M21",
          "text": "I am not as deep into pricing, but I checked the summary tab in A2.\nFrom a delivery cost perspective, the assumptions look reasonable, but I want to flag that if suppliers push back on their rates later, the margin could shrink.\nMaybe we should add a note in T3 that supplier cost changes are a risk to the margin, and link it to the supplier work in T4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T3",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            6784,
            82217
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 90589,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "The target range of 32 to 38 percent and a hard floor at 30 percent works for me.\nIt gives us enough room to compete while keeping a clear rule for exceptions.\nFor communication to sales, we should keep the message simple: standard discounts by segment and a clear minimum margin they cannot cross without approval.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            6784
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 82217,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "I am comfortable with that structure.\nFor the project documentation in A6, I will record:\n- Target margin range: 32 to 38 percent.\n- Minimum margin per bundle: 30 percent, with finance approval required below that.\nThis will also help when we do the go/no-go review later.\nSo I support locking these as our guardrails.",

          "speaker_id": 447542,

          "text": "Aligned with the proposed guardrails.\nI will double-check the formulas in A2 to ensure the margin floor is correctly calculated for each bundle and segment.\nIf I spot any anomalies, I will comment directly in the sheet.",

          "speaker_id": 6784,
          "reply_to": "M21",
          "text": "Thanks for the feedback.\nI will now update A2 to reflect:\n- Target margin range 32 to 38 percent.\n- Hard minimum margin per bundle at 30 percent.\n- Standard and exception discount bands by segment, with finance approval required below the margin floor.\nThis will complete the core of T3 before we take it to finance for sign-off.",

          "text": "Next step is to agree on the initial price list that will go into the sales materials and one-pagers.\nBased on A2, I propose we:\n- Use the list prices in the 'MVP bundles' tab as the official starting point.\n- Include only the standard discount bands in the sales documentation, and keep the exception rules in an internal note.\nIf we all agree, I will mark this as the initial price list for inclusion in the sales enablement work and log it in A6.",

          "text": "Starting the supplier and systems readiness alignment for the Launch of Unified B2B Service Bundles.\nI have updated the integrated project plan and RAID log in A6, and added a first draft of the supplier engagement view in A5, linked to T4 and T7.\nHighlights:\n- Key suppliers mapped to each MVP bundle, with proposed SLA changes.\n- Initial list of contracts that might need updates.\n- Draft scope for ERP and billing changes under T7.\nPlease review A5 and the relevant sections in A6 so we can confirm which supplier contracts must be updated before launch and what we consider as go or no-go criteria for ERP and billing.",

          "text": "I checked A5.\nFor Connectivity Core and Connectivity Plus, the main network supplier is already on 8x5 SLAs, but we are proposing extended hours in the MVP.\nThat means we definitely need to update that contract.\nFor Managed Workplace, the hardware supplier terms seem fine as is.\nSo at minimum, I would say the network supplier contract is a must-update before launch.\nDo we also need to touch the backup connectivity supplier, or can that wait?",

          "text": "Looking at A5, I also see a proposed change for the remote support outsourcing partner to cover extended hours.\nDo we have any indication from them that they can take this on within the current budget, or is that still an open negotiation?\nIf it is not confirmed, we should flag it as a dependency in A6 under T4.",

        {

          "speaker_id": 90589,
          "reply_to": "M37",
          "text": "From a customer promise perspective, the key is that whatever we put in A1 and in the GTM materials is fully backed by supplier SLAs.\nSo I would say any supplier that underpins the extended hours support or the managed services in the MVP bundles must have updated contracts before launch.\nOptional add-ons or roadmap features can wait.\nMaybe we can list those critical suppliers explicitly in A5 as 'must-update before launch'.",

          "speaker_id": 6784,
          "reply_to": "M42",
          "text": "Agree.\nBased on A5 and the MVP bundle definitions in A1, I propose the following list of supplier contracts that must be updated before launch:\n- Primary network supplier (to align to extended hours SLA for Connectivity Core and Plus).\n- Remote support outsourcing partner (to cover extended hours for Support Priority, subject to budget).\n- Cloud service provider for Managed Workplace monitoring (to confirm data retention and reporting terms).\nAll other suppliers can be handled post-launch.\nIf we align on this, we can record it as our confirmed list.",

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.

A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.

* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.

          "speaker_id": 40035,
          "reply_to": "M1",
          "text": "On my side, for full pallet FMCG trucks:\n- I check the delivery note and look at the route sequence if it is printed, but often it is not.\n- I place the first drop pallets near the door so they come off first, but sometimes dispatch asks to change it last minute.\n- Weight wise, I try to keep the center of gravity low and close to the trailer axles, but we do not have a clear rule posted.\nStacking:\n- Max 3 layers on the weaker pallets, 4 on the stronger ones, based on what I have seen, not on a written rule.\nCleaning:\n- We clear plastic wrap and broken wood when it starts to pile up, not on a fixed schedule.\nMain issues: plastic wrap on the floor near the dock edge, and pallets left in the forklift path.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": []
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M4",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": "M1",
          "text": "From the factory hand side:\n- Between trucks we usually just move obvious obstacles out of the way so movers can keep loading.\n- Proper sweeping of ramps and checking emergency exits tends to happen once per shift, often at the end.\n- No formal checklist for floors, ramps, equipment, exits; it is more whoever notices something.\nPain points:\n- Oil spots near the dock plates stay there too long.\n- Some blind corners where forklifts and people cross without markings.\nThis will be useful input when we design the checklist for T4 and later the tracker in T11.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T4",
            "T11",
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M5",
          "speaker_id": 366315,
          "reply_to": "M1",
          "text": "Adding what I see on raw materials trucks:\n- For heavy raw materials, we often unload from the middle first if that is where the forklift can reach best, not always front to back.\n- We sometimes double-stack pallets in the staging area to save space, even when the bottom pallet looks a bit tired.\n- For cleaning, I usually sweep around the staging area when I have a gap, but there is no set time.\nBiggest issues:\n- Broken boards left on the floor.\n- Shrink wrap tails getting caught under wheels.\n- No clear rule on where to park empty pallets, so they end up near the dock edge.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": []
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M6",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M2",
          "text": "Thanks, this helps for T1.\nI am hearing a few patterns:\n- Weight and stacking are mostly based on experience, not a posted rule.\n- Cleaning is reactive, not on a fixed routine.\n- Special loads like dangerous goods and animals are handled case by case.\nTo move forward, we need to pick which load types and routes we focus on first for mapping and later for the pilot.\nMy proposal:\n1) Mixed pallet FMCG route with multiple drops.\n2) Raw materials inbound route with heavy pallets.\n3) One special load type, either dangerous goods or animals.\nCan you all say which of these gives us the most impact if we start there?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            27041,
            40035,
            72769,
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M7",
          "speaker_id": 27041,
          "reply_to": "M6",
          "text": "For me, the mixed pallet FMCG with multiple drops is where we lose the most time.\nWe often reshuffle pallets at the first stop because the order is not right.\nI would vote to start with that route and also include animals, since I handle those sometimes and I am never fully sure about the exact rules.\nRaw materials are heavy but usually more straightforward once the forklift is in place.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M8",
          "speaker_id": 40035,
          "reply_to": "M6",
          "text": "I agree on the mixed pallet multi-drop route as first priority.\nFor the second, I would pick raw materials inbound because of the weight and the risk when we unload from the middle.\nFor special loads, maybe we can document both dangerous goods and animals later under T12, but for the first mapping I would keep it to one so we do not slow down.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M9",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": "M6",
          "text": "From what I see on the floor, the biggest near misses are:\n- Mixed pallet trucks where people walk into the forklift path to find a pallet.\n- Raw materials where the floor is dirty and the load is very heavy.\nI would support focusing on:\n1) Mixed pallet multi-drop.\n2) Raw materials inbound.\nFor special loads, animals are more visible and we already have some habits, while dangerous goods pictograms are often misunderstood.\nMaybe we pick dangerous goods as the special case to map first, then add animals when we work on T12.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M10",
          "speaker_id": 366315,
          "reply_to": "M6",
          "text": "I am ok with starting on mixed pallet multi-drop and raw materials inbound.\nThose are the ones where I see the most broken pallets and messy staging.\nOn special loads, I lean toward dangerous goods first because of the pictograms and the extra rules.\nWe can still note down what we do for animals so we do not forget it when we get to T12.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M11",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M10",
          "text": "Sounds like we are converging.\nLet me play it back to be sure we are aligned before I lock it into the T1 mapping and later into A5 for the pilot:\n- Route 1: mixed pallet multi-drop outbound.\n- Route 2: heavy raw materials inbound.\n- Special load focus: dangerous goods, with animals noted for later.\nIf no one objects, I will treat this as our focus set for the first round of mapping and procedures.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D1"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            27041,
            40035,
            72769,
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M12",
          "speaker_id": 27041,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "No objection from me.\nThose three cases cover most of my day.\nOnce you have the first draft of the T1 map, I can check if the steps match what we actually do when we are under time pressure.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D1"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M13",
          "speaker_id": 40035,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "Works for me as well.\nWhen you share the T1 map, I will add any shortcuts I see people taking, especially around stacking and quick cleaning between trucks.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D1"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M14",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "Agreed.\nFrom the cleaning side, I will note what we currently do on those two routes so we can later compare with the new checklist and what we log in A5 during the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D1"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M15",
          "speaker_id": 366315,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "All good for me.\nI will pay attention this week on raw materials trucks and note any unsafe stacking or cleaning gaps so we can feed that into T1.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D1"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M16",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M15",
          "text": "Great, thanks all.\nI will draft the current-state step list for those two routes plus dangerous goods and share a simple flow for review.\nWe will then be ready to move into drafting the SOP and guidelines.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D1"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            27041,
            40035
          ]
        }
      ],
      "thread_outcome": {

    {
      "thread_id": "TH2",
      "messages": [
        {
          "msg_id": "M17",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have pulled together a first version of the loading and unloading SOP and the stacking rules based on what we mapped in T1.\nSummary:\n- A1 covers pre-checks, loading, unloading and post-checks for the two main routes plus dangerous goods.\n- A2 lists max layers and weight hints per pallet type, plus some examples for mixed loads.\n- For special loads, I started a draft under T12 that will later feed into A6.\nCan you all review with these questions in mind:\n1) Are any key steps missing or out of order in A1?\n2) Are the stacking limits in A2 realistic for what we see on the floor?\n3) Anything unclear or too long for quick use on the dock?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "T2",
            "T3",
            "T12",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            27041,
            40035,
            72769,
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M18",
          "speaker_id": 27041,
          "reply_to": "M17",
          "text": "I went through A1 quickly.\nWhat I like:\n- The pre-check on floor condition and dock plate is clear.\n- The step about confirming route sequence before loading is good.\nQuestions:\n- In the unloading section for raw materials, it says we should always start from the front of the trailer.\nSometimes we cannot reach the front first because of how the truck is parked.\nShould we allow starting from the middle if we secure the load first?\nOn A2, the max layers for the blue pallets look a bit low compared to what we do now.\nWe often go one layer higher without issues, but maybe that is risky.\nNot sure how strict we want to be for the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M19",
          "speaker_id": 40035,
          "reply_to": "M17",
          "text": "I read A1 and A2 as well.\nOn A1:\n- The dangerous goods section mentions checking pictograms but does not say what to do if the label is damaged or missing.\nMaybe add a step to stop and call the supervisor or safety officer.\nOn A2:\n- The examples for mixed loads are helpful, but I would add one case where we have heavy boxes on light pallets stacked on top of stronger pallets.\nThat happens a lot.\nFor T2 and T3, I think the structure is good, but we might need a shorter quick-reference version for the dock wall later.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "T2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M20",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": "M17",
          "text": "From the factory hand side, A1 looks workable.\nThe pre-checks and post-checks are clear enough that we can support movers.\nOne thing: the cleaning step after each truck might be too heavy if we do a full sweep every time.\nMaybe we can define a quick between-truck clean and a deeper clean per shift.\nOn A2, I like that it mentions not stacking damaged pallets, but maybe we should say what to do with them: move to a repair or scrap area.\nFor T12 and A6, I can help later with the animal transport part when we get there.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "T12",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M21",
          "speaker_id": 366315,
          "reply_to": "M17",
          "text": "I checked A2 in detail.\nThe weight hints per pallet type look reasonable from what I see on raw materials.\nI agree with the comment that we sometimes go one layer higher today.\nFor the pilot, I would rather stay on the safe side and then adjust if it slows us down too much.\nOn A1, the step about coordinating with maintenance if equipment looks damaged is good, but maybe we should say to park the forklift out of use until checked.\nThat will avoid people using it anyway.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M22",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M18",
          "text": "Thanks for the detailed reads.\nLet me propose some tweaks based on your points:\n- For raw materials unloading in A1, change the rule to: start from the front when reachable; if not, secure remaining load and then unload from the middle with extra care.\n- For dangerous goods, add a step: if pictogram or label is damaged or missing, stop loading and call supervisor or safety officer.\n- For cleaning, define two levels: quick between-truck clean and deeper per-shift clean.\n- For A2 stacking limits, keep the conservative limits for the pilot, but add a note that we will review after we see data in A5.\nAny objections to these changes before I update T2 and T3 drafts?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "T2",
            "T3",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            27041,
            40035,
            72769,
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M23",
          "speaker_id": 27041,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "Those changes work for me.\nThe flexibility on unloading from the middle matches what we actually do, and the extra care note is a good reminder.\nKeeping the stricter stacking limits for the pilot is fine as long as we really review them later with A5 data.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M24",
          "speaker_id": 40035,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "I am aligned with those tweaks.\nPlease also add that damaged labels on dangerous goods mean we do not move the pallet until someone with authority clears it.\nOn the quick vs deep clean, maybe we can later mirror that in the cleaning checklist A3 so it is consistent.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M25",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "No objections.\nThe two-level cleaning approach will help us keep up with operations.\nWhen we get to A3, we can spell out which items are between-truck and which are per-shift.\nFor A2, I like the idea of reviewing limits after the pilot using A5.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 366315,
          "reply_to": "M22",
          "text": "All good from my side.\nParking damaged forklifts out of use until checked should be clearly written in A1.\nFor T3, maybe add a simple visual in A2 showing good vs bad stacking on damaged pallets.\nThat will help people decide quickly.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "I have now applied these changes to the T2 SOP draft and the T3 stacking guideline, and updated A1 and A2 accordingly.\nBefore we move to the pilot, we need to be clear that we are ok using these versions as our test standard.\nTo summarise what we would approve for the pilot:\n- A1: includes flexible unloading rule, clear stop-and-call step for dangerous goods labels, and equipment out-of-use rule.\n- A2: conservative stacking limits, damaged pallet rule, and mixed-load examples.\nAre you comfortable treating A1 as the SOP for the pilot week and A2 as the stacking rules we will follow during that period?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "T2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            27041,
            40035,
            72769,
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 27041,
          "reply_to": "M27",
          "text": "Yes, I am ok using A1 as the SOP for the pilot.\nThe steps are clear enough that I can follow them even when it is busy.\nFor A2, I will stick to the limits during the pilot and note any cases where it really slows us down so we can log them in A5.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D2",
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 40035,
          "reply_to": "M27",
          "text": "Same here, I am comfortable with A1 and A2 as pilot standards.\nWe just need to make sure everyone on shift has a quick way to see the key points, maybe a one-page summary later.\nFor now, I will follow A1 and A2 as written during the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D2",
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            18289
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M30",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": "M27",
          "text": "Agreed from my side.\nI will support movers in following A1 and A2 during the pilot and help capture any issues in A5.\nLater, when we expand T12 and A6 for special loads, we can build on this base.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A5",
            "T12",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D2",
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M31",
          "speaker_id": 366315,
          "reply_to": "M27",
          "text": "I am on board as well.\nUsing A1 and A2 consistently during the pilot will give us good data in A5 to decide if any limits can be relaxed without losing safety.\nNo further changes from me before the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D2",
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M32",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M31",
          "text": "Thanks all.\nWe will treat the current A1 as the approved SOP draft for the pilot and A2 as the stacking and weight distribution rules to apply.\nI will freeze the T2 and T3 versions for the pilot and note any changes after we review A5.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1",
            "A2",
            "T2",
            "T3",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D2",

    {
      "thread_id": "TH3",
      "messages": [
        {
          "msg_id": "M33",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have drafted a proposal for the new cleaning checklist and the tracking sheet.\n- A3: daily loading bay cleaning and inspection list, split into between-truck quick tasks and per-shift deeper tasks.\n- A8: simple tracker with date, shift, completed items and issues.\nThese are linked to T4 and T11.\nKey points in A3:\n- Floors and ramps: quick sweep between trucks if debris or spills, full sweep and spot clean once per shift.\n- Equipment: visual check of forklifts and dock plates once per shift, note issues in A8.\n- Emergency exits: check clear once per shift.\nPlease review and tell me if the tasks and timing look realistic for your shifts.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A8",
            "T4",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289,
            27041,
            40035,
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M34",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "Thanks for putting this together.\nOn A3, the split between quick and per-shift tasks matches what we discussed in A1.\nQuestions from the mover side:\n- For between-truck quick sweep, who is responsible if we are in the middle of a rush, mover or factory hand?\n- For equipment visual checks, should we tie that to the first truck of each shift so it does not get forgotten?\nOn A8, I like the simple columns.\nMaybe we should add a short free-text field for near-misses so we can later cross-check with A5 during the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A8",
            "A1",
            "A5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M35",
          "speaker_id": 27041,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "Looking at A3 from my shift:\n- Quick sweep between trucks is fine most of the time, but when we have three trucks waiting it will be hard to do more than push debris aside.\n- The per-shift deep clean might be better placed at the end of the shift, not mid-shift.\nOn A8, I am ok filling it in, but it needs to be somewhere we pass by anyway, like near the time clock or the dock entrance.\nOtherwise people will forget.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 40035,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "A3 looks good overall.\nI would add a specific line for removing plastic wrap and broken boards from the dock edge.\nThat is one of our biggest trip hazards.\nFor A8, could we have a simple tick box for each shift to say: quick tasks done, deep tasks done, issues logged?\nThat way we do not have to write too much when it is busy.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M37",
          "speaker_id": 366315,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "From the factory hand side, the workload in A3 seems manageable if we spread tasks across shifts.\nI suggest:\n- Early shift: focus on ramps and exits.\n- Late shift: deeper clean of staging areas.\nOn A8, I agree with placing it where everyone passes.\nWe could also use different pen colors per shift so it is easy to see who filled what.\nFor T11, that should still count as a simple tracking method.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A8",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 72769,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "Good points.\nProposal to refine A3 and A8:\n- Responsibility: quick between-truck sweep done by whoever finishes the load, usually the mover, with factory hand stepping in when there is a queue.\n- Equipment visual checks: tie them to the first truck of each shift, with a note in A3.\n- Add explicit line for plastic wrap and broken boards removal.\n- In A8, add tick boxes for quick and deep tasks, plus a short free-text field for near-misses.\nWe can mount A8 on a board near the dock entrance so everyone sees it.\nDoes this sound workable before we lock the checklist content?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            18289,
            27041,
            40035,
            366315
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 18289,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "Works for me.\nTying equipment checks to the first truck of the shift will make it easier to remember.\nI can help remind movers during the first week.\nMounting A8 near the dock entrance is also good, we all pass there.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "A8"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            72769
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M40",

2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

IMPORTANT: You will use the participants' information [INPUT PARTICIPANTS] as a basis to try to infer the skill, productivity, and performance levels of each participant. Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:
   * Messages where speaker_id == the participant’s _id.
   * If the participant speaks little, you can also use messages that mention them (mentions contains _id) as contextual evidence.
2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of HIGH => candidate HIGH
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of LOW  => candidate LOW
   * otherwise => MID
3. Attention:
   * If there are strong signals of HIGH and LOW at the same time for the same attribute, choose MID (conservative rule).
   * In the corporate context, everyone needs to deliver and demonstrate work; be careful to infer HIGH for something standard that should be MID.
   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:
   * If there are no messages from the participant, use MID for all three attributes and use evidence from a message where they were mentioned.

EVIDENCE RULES (MANDATORY)
* For each participant, return 2 to 5 items in evidence.
* Each evidence item:
  * attribute ∈ {"productivity","ability","performance"}
  * msg_id must exist in the channel
  * justification: one sentence justifying the label.
  * snippet must be a short quote (up to ~20 words) copied from the text of that msg (no comment).
* Do not invent msg_id.
* Do not include “LOW/MID/HIGH” in the snippet.

  ]
}

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)

* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.

* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

          "speaker_id": 49338,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "Looking at A4 from an operator point of view, it would help if we have simple steps posted at each station:\n- How to stop the machine in an emergency\n- Who to call before touching any guards or panels\n- Basic do and do not items.\nWe can keep the detailed lockout steps in A4, but a short version near the machines will avoid confusion.",

          "text": "The proposed sequence works for me.\nI will adjust A2 to:\n1) Place and level PCB bench\n2) Place and level press and test bench\n3) Connect power and air\n4) Run individual test runs\n5) Run integrated dry run with mock parts.\nFor T8 and A4, I will add a section on who can perform lockout and where keys are stored, plus a short operator-facing summary as suggested.",

          "msg_id": "M53",
          "speaker_id": 416835,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have drafted the initial relocation and downtime plan based on T5 and T10 and captured it in A7.\nKey points:\n- Move PCB bench on Day 1 during the last two hours of the shift\n- Move press and test bench on Day 2 during a planned 3-hour window\n- Use pallet jack and small crane, with two movers and one mechanic present\n- Keep a manual backup station outside the new cell to cover urgent orders.\nMaterial routes in A1 are updated so inbound and outbound do not cross.\nPlease review the schedule and resource assumptions.",

          "speaker_id": 557389,

          "text": "I agree the timing is tight.\nTo reduce risk, I suggest we:\n- Disconnect and label cables and hoses at the end of the previous shift\n- Have all anchors and leveling tools staged in the new cell.\nI can support the Day 2 move and quick test runs as described in A2 so we do not extend downtime.",

          "reply_to": "M53",
          "text": "From the cell owner view, the sequence in A7 looks ok as long as:\n- We keep at least one PCB and one mechanical station running outside the new cell until the final test bench is live\n- Material staging in T5 is ready before we start the moves.\nI would like to avoid any full stop longer than the planned windows.",

          "speaker_id": 49338,
          "reply_to": "M53",
          "text": "For mechanical assembly, as long as we have the manual backup station with torque tools and basic fixtures, we can keep building at a reduced rate during the move.\nWe just need clear instructions on when to switch from old to new cell so operators do not get confused.",

          "speaker_id": 89646,
          "reply_to": "M53",
          "text": "On PCB, I can work with a temporary bench if needed, but it is better if we move the main PCB bench first as you planned.\nIf we keep the continuity tester available during the move, we can still catch obvious issues before boards go to mechanical.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A7"

            416835
          ]

        {
          "msg_id": "M59",
          "speaker_id": 416835,
          "reply_to": "M54",
          "text": "Good points.\nI will update A7 and T10 to:\n- Include pre-disconnect and labeling at the end of the previous shift\n- Stage anchors, leveling tools, and lifting gear in the new cell before the move windows.\nFor T5, I will also mark temporary staging zones so we do not block aisles while machines are in transit.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          "mentions": [
            55482,
            557389
          ]

          "msg_id": "M60",
          "speaker_id": 55482,
          "reply_to": "M59",
          "text": "With those adjustments, I am comfortable with the schedule.\nWe just need to make sure the lockout steps from A4 are followed during disconnect and reconnect.\nI will brief the mechanics team on that.",
