          "msg_id": "M72",
          "speaker_id": 357710,
          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "Looking at the notes in A6 and the early feedback for T11, households seemed appreciative of both the food and the check-in. A couple of people mentioned that they liked knowing roughly when we would come. On the expiry issue, I wonder if we need a second date check step in A3 just before loading, in addition to the one during packing under T6.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "T11",
            "A3",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            429831,
            44809
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M73",
          "speaker_id": 44809,
          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "On the packing side, the checklist in A3 worked, but we were a bit rushed and I can see how the near-expiry item slipped through. For T6, I suggest we add a simple rule: if an item is within two days of expiry on delivery day, it does not go into a parcel. We can also assign one person to do a final visual check of each parcel before it is staged.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T6",
            "A7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            429831
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M74",
          "speaker_id": 534740,
          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "From the logs in A6, the coding scheme from A5 worked well; there were no mix-ups between households. For T11, I noticed that we used the CR code for concern raised twice. It might help if we agree on a simple follow-up process for those cases, so that they do not get lost between weeks.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "A5",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            357710
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M75",
          "speaker_id": 429831,
          "reply_to": "M73",
          "text": "I support adding the two-day rule to A3 and T6. It is a simple change that should reduce the risk of borderline items going out. We can also highlight this in A2 so that everyone is aware.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T6",
            "A2"

          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            44809

        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M76",
          "speaker_id": 516425,
          "reply_to": "M71",
          "text": "On route timing, I can adjust T4 so that each route has one fewer household than the maximum we think we can handle, leaving more buffer.           "artifact_refs": [
            "T4",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            357710,
            429831
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M77",
          "speaker_id": 357710,
          "reply_to": "M74",
          "text": "For the CR cases in A6, I suggest a simple follow-up rule for T11: any concern raised is reviewed by me within two working days, and, if needed, passed on to the community social work team using existing referral routes. We do not record detailed information in A6, just enough to know that a follow-up is needed.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            534740
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M78",
          "speaker_id": 44809,
          "reply_to": "M72",
          "text": "I can update A3 to include the second date check just before loading, as you suggested. That way, even if something slips through during packing, we have another chance to catch it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            357710,
            429831
          ]
        },

          "msg_id": "M79",
          "speaker_id": 516425,
          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "On the script in A4, I found that being explicit about time helped: saying something like, 'I will just take a couple of minutes to check how things are going' set expectations. Maybe we can add that line to the opening in A4 so that staff feel more comfortable keeping visits short.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            357710
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M80",
          "speaker_id": 357710,
          "reply_to": "M79",
          "text": "That is a good tweak. I will adjust A4 under T5 to include a brief mention of time in the opening line, so households know this is a short check-in.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            516425
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M81",
          "speaker_id": 534740,
          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "From a data perspective, the dry run gave us enough to test A6 and the coding scheme in A5, and both held up. For T11, I will start pulling a short weekly summary from A6 once the full pilot starts, focusing on delivery counts, missed deliveries, and CR cases.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "A5",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            357710
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M82",
          "speaker_id": 429831,
          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "To help us decide on D8, here is a quick recap of the main adjustments we are proposing: 1) Strengthen A3 and T6 with a two-day expiry rule and a second date check before loading. 2) Adjust T4 to cap routes at around 8 households to allow more buffer. 3) Slightly tweak A4 to set expectations about visit length. 4) Use the CR follow-up rule in A6 and T11. With these changes, I believe the process is safe and manageable enough to proceed with the full 6-week pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T6",
            "T4",
            "A4",
            "A6",
            "T11",
            "A7"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D8"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            516425,
            357710,
            44809,
            534740
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M83",
          "speaker_id": 516425,
          "reply_to": "M82",
          "text": "I support going ahead with the full pilot under D8, with the adjustments you listed. From the delivery side, the changes to T4 and A4 should make the weekly rounds more sustainable.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T4",
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D8"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            429831
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M84",
          "speaker_id": 357710,

          "text": "Sharing the initial pricing model and tier proposal for the pilot, based on A2, T4, and T5.\nAssumptions from A1 and TH1:\n- Primary segment: mid-market customers with existing integrations, at least 6 months of data, and a minimum recurring revenue threshold.\n- MVP feature set: unified subscription dashboard (revenue and active subscriptions), basic login activity metric, hybrid onboarding.\nProposed tiers for the pilot:\n- Core: includes the MVP dashboard and standard onboarding; priced as a percentage of monthly recurring revenue with a minimum monthly fee.\n- Plus: same as Core, plus priority support and early access to future analytics features; higher percentage and higher minimum.\nFor discounts, the draft in A5 suggests:\n- Standard volume discounts up to a certain percentage, approved by sales management\n- Anything above that threshold requires approval from finance and product leadership\nI would like feedback on whether two tiers are enough for the pilot and whether the discount thresholds feel realistic for our sales motion.",

          "speaker_id": 22473,
          "reply_to": "M33",

            "A1",
            "A6",

          "speaker_id": 94563,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "Looking at this from the customer and data side, two tiers should be enough for the pilot, especially since the feature set is still lean.\nFor T2 and T8, it would help to have clear criteria for which customers we expect to land in Core versus Plus. For example, we could map Plus to customers with higher recurring revenue and more complex internal stakeholders, where priority support is more valuable.\nOn discounts, I would like to understand how the proposed thresholds in A5 compare to our current discount patterns. If we set them too low, we might create friction with the sales team.",

            "T2",

          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 242297,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "From an operational and staffing perspective, I am cautious about promising too much on the Plus tier.\nPriority support and early access to future analytics features will require clear processes in T6 and T11, and we need to be sure we can handle that with existing teams.\nFor the pilot, I would suggest we define priority support as a specific response time and a named point of contact, rather than a broad promise. That way we can design the onboarding checklist in A4 and the RACI in T11 to support it without overcommitting.",

          "speaker_id": 132848,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "On your questions:\n- For the Core tier minimum fee, the draft in A2 assumes a floor that is a small fraction of the minimum recurring revenue threshold for the target segment. This keeps the product meaningful in terms of revenue while still accessible to smaller mid-market accounts.\n- For Plus, I agree we need to be precise. For the pilot, I propose we define priority support as a shorter response time and a dedicated email alias, not a separate team. Early access would mean they are first in line when we roll out new analytics features after the pilot, not that we build custom features.\nIf we align on these definitions, I am comfortable keeping the two-tier structure for the pilot.",

          "speaker_id": 132848,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "On discount thresholds in A5, I benchmarked against our current discount patterns and internal revenue policies.\nThe draft suggests:\n- Sales can approve discounts up to a certain percentage off list price for both tiers, as long as the deal meets the minimum fee and target segment criteria.\n- Discounts above that threshold require approval from finance and product leadership, to ensure we do not erode the business case in A2.\nFor the pilot, we could keep the thresholds slightly more flexible, but I would still like a clear rule so that we can measure the impact on revenue in T4.",

        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 22473,
          "reply_to": "M37",
          "text": "The definitions you propose for priority support and early access sound workable for the pilot.\nFor the tier structure, I am leaning toward keeping just Core and Plus for now, with clear mapping rules for T8 so that we know which pilot customers we expect in each tier.\nUnless others see a strong need for a third tier during the pilot, I would suggest we confirm the two-tier model and focus on testing price points and discount behaviour.",

          "speaker_id": 94563,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "I am comfortable with two tiers for the pilot.\nFor T2 and T8, I will document that:\n- Core is the default for eligible mid-market customers\n- Plus is targeted at higher recurring revenue customers or those with more complex needs, where priority support and early access are more valuable\nThis should also help sales and customer success understand which customers to propose each tier to, once A6 is ready.",

          "speaker_id": 242297,

          "text": "Two tiers are easier to operationalise for the pilot.\nFrom a process standpoint, we can design onboarding and support workflows in T6 and T11 that differentiate clearly between Core and Plus, without adding too much complexity.\nI support confirming the two-tier model for the pilot and revisiting the need for additional tiers after we see pilot results.",

          "msg_id": "M63",
          "speaker_id": 22473,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Sharing an early view of pilot KPIs and customer feedback, based on A8, T10, and T12.\nHeadline metrics so far:\n- Attach rate: a meaningful percentage of eligible mid-market customers have adopted the subscription product.\n- Revenue: pilot monthly recurring revenue is tracking slightly above the base scenario in A2.\n- Usage: most pilot customers show regular logins, but a subset have low activity despite being live.\nQualitative feedback:\n- Customers value the unified view of revenue and active subscriptions.\n- Several have asked for more granular segmentation and cohort analysis.\n- Onboarding feedback is generally positive, but some Plus customers expect even faster responses.\nI would like us to discuss whether we should expand the product beyond the pilot, iterate on scope, or pause to address gaps before scaling. This will feed directly into the roadmap proposal in T12.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "T10",
            "T12",
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            94563,

        {
          "msg_id": "M64",
          "speaker_id": 94563,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "Looking at the KPIs in A8 and the data from T10, I see a few patterns:\n- Customers with higher recurring revenue tend to have higher login activity, especially in the Plus tier.\n- The low-activity customers often have multiple internal stakeholders who have not all been onboarded.\nFrom a next-phase perspective, I would suggest we:\n- Expand the pilot to a limited additional set of customers that match the high-usage profile.\n- Add roadmap items in T12 to improve onboarding for multi-stakeholder accounts and to explore more granular analytics.\nI do not see a reason to pause, but we should be deliberate about where we expand.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "T10",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            22473
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M65",
          "speaker_id": 132848,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "From the business case side, comparing the pilot results to A2:\n- Revenue performance above the base scenario is a strong signal to continue and expand, provided we can maintain attach rates and discount discipline.\n- The cost to serve for Plus customers is slightly higher than expected, mainly due to support expectations, but still within an acceptable range.\nGiven this, my recommendation is to expand the product beyond the initial pilot, while prioritising roadmap items in T12 that:\n- Address the most common feature requests (segmentation and cohorts)\n- Optimise onboarding and support for Plus customers\nI do not see a case for pausing, but we should avoid a full-scale rollout until we have at least one iteration on the feature set.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T4",
            "T5",
            "T12"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            22473,
            242297

        {
          "msg_id": "M66",
          "speaker_id": 242297,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "Operationally, the onboarding checklist in A4 and the RACI in T11 have held up reasonably well.\nWe have seen some strain on the team for Plus customers, especially around response times, but nothing unmanageable.\nBefore a broader rollout, I would like T12 to include:\n- A refinement of the onboarding process for multi-stakeholder accounts\n- Clearer guidelines for handling Plus support requests, possibly with better tooling\nGiven the current results, I support expanding the product, but in a controlled way, while we iterate on these processes.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T6",
            "T11",
            "T12"
          ],

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "We have completed the pilots on Line A and Line B. I compiled the results and feedback into A8 for T12, including uptime improvements, installation notes, and issues found.             "A3",

          "msg_id": "M64",
          "speaker_id": 81818,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "From the application side, the pilot customers appreciated the visibility into machine states and alerts, but they asked for simpler configuration flows and clearer guidance.             "A6",
            "T9",
            "A8"

            29405

          "msg_id": "M65",
          "speaker_id": 59849,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "Looking at the data in A8, the edge software in T5 behaved as expected most of the time, but we did see a few cases where network outages caused longer delays than we wanted. For the next iteration, I suggest we improve the retry strategy and add clearer indicators in the backend when data is delayed, so users do not confuse it with sensor failures.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A8",
            "T5"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            81818
          ]
        },

          "msg_id": "M66",
          "speaker_id": 219209,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "On the electrical side, the pilots confirmed that the 24 VDC only approach and the current channel counts are acceptable for many use cases. For now, I would keep the hardware as is and focus on improving wiring instructions and labeling in the documentation.",

            "A8",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            29405,
            81818

          "msg_id": "M67",
          "speaker_id": 249439,
          "reply_to": "M63",
          "text": "Mechanically, the enclosure and mounting concept held up well. The only recurring comment in A8 was that access to some terminals was a bit tight in crowded cabinets.             "T2"

            219209

          "speaker_id": 29405,
          "reply_to": "M64",
          "text": "On cost, the BOM analysis in A3 and T8 shows we are slightly above the target ceiling, mainly due to the enclosure and pluggable terminals.             "A3",
            "T8",

          "speaker_id": 81818,
          "reply_to": "M68",
          "text": "Given the positive impact on downtime and the feedback on usability, I propose that the next iteration scope in T12 focuses on three areas: refine configuration UX and templates, improve documentation and playbook in A6 and T9, and pursue targeted cost reductions that do not compromise reliability.           "speaker_id": 59849,

* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:
   * Messages where speaker_id == the participant’s _id.
   * If the participant speaks little, you can also use messages that mention them (mentions contains _id) as contextual evidence.
2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of HIGH => candidate HIGH
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of LOW  => candidate LOW
   * otherwise => MID
3. Attention:
   * If there are strong signals of HIGH and LOW at the same time for the same attribute, choose MID (conservative rule).
   * In the corporate context, everyone needs to deliver and demonstrate work; be careful to infer HIGH for something standard that should be MID.
   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:
   * If there are no messages from the participant, use MID for all three attributes and use evidence from a message where they were mentioned.

EVIDENCE RULES (MANDATORY)
* For each participant, return 2 to 5 items in evidence.
* Each evidence item:
  * attribute ∈ {"productivity","ability","performance"}
  * msg_id must exist in the channel
  * justification: one sentence justifying the label.
  * snippet must be a short quote (up to ~20 words) copied from the text of that msg (no comment).
* Do not invent msg_id.
* Do not include “LOW/MID/HIGH” in the snippet.

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.

        {

          "speaker_id": 47068,
          "reply_to": "M7",
          "text": "For in-home and workshop appliance repairs, my top three would be:\n1) Parts not available when needed, leading to second visits\n2) Time pressure from tight scheduling, especially when travel or complex diagnosis is involved\n3) Paper forms not matching what customer service promises, so expectations are misaligned\nOn the maps, the only thing that feels off is that the safety check is shown after opening the appliance. In practice, I do a quick environment and power check before touching anything.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M9",
          "speaker_id": 61983,
          "reply_to": "M7",
          "text": "For power tools, my top three pain points are:\n1) Poor intake information and missing accessories, which slows down diagnostics\n2) Rework due to incomplete documentation of tests and repairs\n3) Storage and tagging issues that delay returning tools to customers\nThe map looks mostly right to me. I agree with the comment about adding a clear test run step before deciding on parts, especially for tools that only fail under load.",

            63344
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M10",
          "speaker_id": 63344,
          "reply_to": "M7",
          "text": "Aligning with what was said for power tools, my three would be:\n1) No clear place to record expected parts delivery dates\n2) Lack of standard way to compare old and new readings when a tool comes back\n3) Confusion when multiple technicians touch the same tool without a shared checklist\nI am ok with you adding a separate test run step in the map. That matches what I do at the bench.",

          ],

            61983
          ]

        {
          "msg_id": "M11",
          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": "M7",
          "text": "For telecom and electronics visits, my top three pain points are:\n1) Appointments booked without checking building or roof access, which can block the job\n2) No standard way to log signal readings and configurations\n3) No clear script for cases where the issue is outside our control, like network outages\nThe map is mostly fine. I would just add a pre-visit system check step and a more explicit logging step after testing.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M12",
          "speaker_id": 319539,
          "reply_to": "M7",
          "text": "From the moving side, my three main pain points are:\n1) Last-minute schedule changes that cause extra trips or idle time\n2) Lack of information about weight, dimensions, and special handling needs when jobs are created\n3) No standard packing and securing checklist for heavy or fragile items\nThe map could show more clearly when we need a technician on-site to disconnect or secure equipment before we move it.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M13",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M11",
          "text": "Thanks all, this is very consistent.\nTo move us toward a shared view, I propose we cluster the pain points into themes:\nA) Intake and documentation quality (missing info, missing accessories, missing readings, unclear labels)\nB) Scheduling and coordination (time windows, last-minute changes, access constraints, mover and technician coordination)\nC) Parts and materials flow (availability, tracking, expected delivery dates)\nIf we had to pick three to focus on in the first version of the standard operating procedure, my suggestion would be:\n1) Intake and documentation quality\n2) Scheduling and coordination\n3) Parts and materials flow\nPlease react or comment if you disagree or would swap any of these.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A1"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            47068,
            61983,
            63344,
            125309,
            319539
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M14",
          "speaker_id": 61983,
          "reply_to": "M13",
          "text": "Those three themes work for me.\nIf we improve intake and documentation, a lot of the rework on power tools should drop. Scheduling and parts flow are also big drivers of delays from what I see at the bench.",
          "artifact_refs": [],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M15",
          "speaker_id": 47068,
          "reply_to": "M13",
          "text": "I agree with those three.\nFor appliances, intake and parts flow are the biggest sources of second visits. Scheduling and coordination also matter, but if we fix the first two, the day already becomes much smoother.",
          "artifact_refs": [],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M16",
          "speaker_id": 319539,
          "reply_to": "M13",
          "text": "From the moving side, I am aligned as well.\nScheduling and coordination is key for us, but it depends a lot on good intake information, so grouping them like this makes sense.",
          "artifact_refs": [],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M17",
          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": "M13",
          "text": "Works for me too.\nIf we standardise how we log readings and pre-visit checks, that should help with both documentation and scheduling for telecom visits.",
          "artifact_refs": [],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M18",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M17",
          "text": "Great, sounds like we have convergence.\nLet us lock in the top three focus areas for the first version of the standard operating procedure as:\n1) Intake and documentation quality\n2) Scheduling and coordination\n3) Parts and materials flow\nOn scope for the initial pilot, my proposal is to include:\n- In-home appliance repairs\n- Workshop power tool repairs\n- Telecom and consumer electronics visits\nWe can bring movers into the pilot where these jobs require transport, but not run a separate mover-only pilot.\nPlease confirm if you are ok with this pilot scope or if you see any major gaps.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          ],
          "decision_refs": [

          ],
          "mentions": [
            47068,

            319539
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M19",
          "speaker_id": 61983,
          "reply_to": "M18",
          "text": "Pilot scope sounds good to me.\nIncluding workshop power tools and the related moves should give us enough volume without overcomplicating things.",
          "artifact_refs": [],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643,
            319539
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M20",
          "speaker_id": 47068,
          "reply_to": "M18",
          "text": "I am ok with that scope.\nIn-home appliance repairs are where we see most of the customer impact, so it makes sense to include them early.",
          "artifact_refs": [],

          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M21",
          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": "M18",
          "text": "Fine by me.\nTelecom and electronics visits fit well into this, and we can test the new logging and communication steps there.",
          "artifact_refs": [],

        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M22",
          "speaker_id": 319539,

          "text": "I am comfortable with movers being part of the pilot where transport is needed, without a separate stream.\nThat should still give us enough data on handling and coordination.",

          "msg_id": "M24",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "Following up on the workflow mapping, I have drafted first versions of the appliance and power tool diagnostic checklists.\nThey are captured as:\n- Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist\n- Power Tool Repair Checklist\nBoth are based on Current Repair Workflow Maps and the pain points we agreed to focus on.\nKey questions:\n1) For each checklist, what are the minimum steps that must always be done on every job?\n2) What should be optional or only for specific fault types?\nPlease review and comment so we can finalise the first versions and move toward pilot-ready checklists.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "T2",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            47068,
            61983,
            63344
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M25",
          "speaker_id": 47068,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "I went through Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist.\nFor me, the steps that should always be done on every appliance job are:\n- Basic safety and environment check (power outlet, water, gas where relevant)\n- Intake confirmation with the customer (symptoms, history, any previous repairs)\n- Visual inspection of the appliance and connections\n- Basic functional test to reproduce the issue\n- Final test after repair and short explanation to the customer\nThe more detailed component-level checks could be conditional based on the symptom.\nOne concern: the checklist has a lot of fields. I am worried it might slow us down if we have to tick every single one on paper.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 61983,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "On Power Tool Repair Checklist, I like that it separates intake, visual, electrical tests, and functional tests.\nMinimum steps I would always do:\n- Intake check: confirm tool type, accessories received, and fault description\n- Visual inspection: housing, cord or battery contacts, obvious damage\n- Basic electrical safety checks before powering on\n- Functional test under no load and, where safe, under load\n- Final test and documentation of readings or observations\nMore advanced tests, like detailed motor diagnostics, could be conditional.\nWe should also make sure there is a clear place to note which accessories were tested, to avoid confusion later.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 63344,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "I reviewed Power Tool Repair Checklist as well.\nI have a question: for battery tools, should we always test both the battery and the charger, or only when the symptom suggests a power issue?\nIf we make it mandatory, it might add time, but if we skip it, we might miss some faults.\nAlso, I did not see a field for expected parts delivery date. Should that be part of this checklist or a separate form?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            61983,
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M27",
          "text": "Good questions.\nOn battery tools, my initial thought is:\n- Always test the battery and charger when the symptom is related to power or runtime\n- Make it optional for purely mechanical issues, but still available on the checklist\nFor expected parts delivery date, I would lean toward adding a field in the checklist so that it is captured consistently, even if the actual ordering happens in another system.\nLet us hear from others on whether that feels workable in practice.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            61983,
            63344
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 61983,
          "reply_to": "M27",
          "text": "On the battery and charger question, I would support making it conditional.\nIf the tool clearly has a mechanical issue, like a broken housing or switch, testing every battery and charger every time might not add much.\nBut we should make the conditional rule very clear in the checklist so people do not skip it when it is relevant.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            63344
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M30",
          "speaker_id": 47068,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "Coming back to Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist, I think we should also include a simple field for parts used and estimated versus actual time.\nThat will help us later when we look at rework and time per job.\nI am still a bit unsure how we will fit all of this on the existing paper forms without making them too crowded.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "T2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M31",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M30",
          "text": "On the paper form constraint, we can prioritise which fields must be on the main form and which can be on the back or as a short code.\nFor appliances, I hear the following as minimum mandatory steps for every job:\n- Safety and environment check\n- Intake confirmation\n- Visual inspection\n- Basic functional test\n- Final test and customer explanation\nCan you confirm if you are comfortable treating these as the non-negotiable core, and making the rest conditional or optional?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            47068
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M32",
          "speaker_id": 47068,
          "reply_to": "M31",
          "text": "Yes, I am comfortable with those as the core steps for every appliance job.\nIf we keep the rest as conditional, it should be manageable on paper.\nWe just need the checklist to be clear about which steps are always required and which depend on the symptom.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M33",
          "speaker_id": 61983,
          "reply_to": "M24",
          "text": "For Power Tool Repair Checklist, I would define the minimum required steps as:\n- Confirm intake details and accessories\n- Visual inspection\n- Basic electrical safety checks\n- Functional test (no load, and under load when safe)\n- Final test and documentation of results\nBattery and charger tests would be mandatory when the symptom suggests a power issue, and optional otherwise.\nIf we agree on that, I think we can move forward with this as the base for the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643,
            63344
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M34",
          "speaker_id": 63344,
          "reply_to": "M33",
          "text": "I am ok with that definition.\nHaving the functional test and documentation as mandatory should help reduce rework when tools come back.\nFor the parts delivery date, could we add a small field near the parts section so it is easy to find?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            61983,
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M35",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M34",
          "text": "Sounds like we have a shared view.\nTo summarise for Power Tool Repair Checklist:\n- Mandatory for every job: intake confirmation, visual inspection, basic electrical safety checks, functional test, final test and documentation\n- Conditional: battery and charger tests when the symptom points to power issues, advanced diagnostics as needed\nWe will also add a field for expected parts delivery date in the parts section.\nIf there are no objections, I will treat this as the agreed minimum set of steps for the pilot version.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D4"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            61983,
            63344
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M36",
          "speaker_id": 61983,
          "reply_to": "M35",
          "text": "No objections from me.\nOnce we start the pilot, I can keep notes on any steps that feel redundant or any missing checks, so we can feed that into the refinement task later.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M37",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M36",
          "text": "Great.\nI will update Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist and Power Tool Repair Checklist with the agreed minimum steps and conditional rules, and we will use these versions for the pilot.\nWe will revisit them after we have some pilot data and feedback to refine and remove any redundant steps.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A2",
            "A3",
            "T2",
            "T3",
            "T11"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D3",
            "D4"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            47068,
            61983,
            63344
          ]
        }
      ],

          "msg_id": "M38",
          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": null,
          "text": "I have put together a draft of the telecom and consumer electronics service visit procedure based on our earlier mapping.\nThe document is Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP.\nIt covers:\n- Pre-visit checks (system status, signal levels where available)\n- On-site installation or repair steps\n- Signal testing and logging\n- Wrap-up and customer communication\nPlease review and let me know if any key steps are missing or out of order, especially around safety and logging.\nIn parallel, we also have a draft Handling and Transport Safety Checklist from the moving side to review.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A6",
            "T4",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643,
            319539
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M39",
          "speaker_id": 319539,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "On Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, I focused on:\n- Packing steps for fragile electronics and heavy appliances\n- Lifting techniques and when to use extra equipment\n- Securing items in the vehicle and coordination with technicians on-site\nFrom my side, the sequence is:\n1) Confirm item details and any special handling notes\n2) Prepare packing materials\n3) Coordinate with technician to disconnect or secure equipment\n4) Lift and move using proper techniques\n5) Secure items in the vehicle following the checklist\nHappy to adjust if there are telecom-specific needs I have not covered.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            125309,
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M40",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M38",
          "text": "Thanks for drafting these.\nFor Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, I want to make sure we are explicit about:\n- Pre-visit checks to avoid wasted trips when there are known outages or access issues\n- Standard fields for logging signal readings and configurations\n- Clear handover when movers are involved in transporting equipment\nCould you walk us through how the logging section works in Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, and where you see the interface with Handling and Transport Safety Checklist?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            125309,
            319539
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M41",
          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": "M40",
          "text": "In Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, the logging section currently has:\n- Fields for initial signal readings (downstream, upstream, noise margin)\n- Configuration notes (router location, SSID, channel, any repeaters installed)\n- Final readings after adjustments\nThe idea is that we log these on the existing paper form using short codes.\nFor the interface with Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, I added a step in the on-site section: if equipment needs to be moved to another room or location, we call out that movers or a second person may be required for heavy items, and we reference the handling checklist.\nI am not fully sure if the access checks before the visit are detailed enough, though.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643,
            319539
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M42",
          "speaker_id": 319539,
          "reply_to": "M41",
          "text": "From the moving side, the interface you describe makes sense.\nIf the SOP clearly states when a second person or mover is required, and links to Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, that should reduce unsafe lifting.\nOne suggestion: in the handling checklist, we can add a simple field to note whether the move is within the same room, same floor, or between floors, since that changes the risk.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            125309
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M43",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M41",
          "text": "On the access checks, I suggest we make the pre-visit section of Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP more explicit:\n- Confirm building or roof access if needed\n- Check for any known network outages in the area\n- Confirm customer contact details and any special instructions\nWould you be comfortable adding these as mandatory pre-visit steps for telecom and electronics jobs in the pilot?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            125309
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M44",
          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": "M43",
          "text": "Yes, I can add those as mandatory pre-visit steps.\nThey match what I try to do already, just not always in a structured way.\nMaking them explicit in Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP should help reduce wasted trips.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M45",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M39",
          "text": "On Handling and Transport Safety Checklist, I like the structure you outlined.\nTo align with our overall safety requirements, we should ensure it includes:\n- Clear guidance on when to refuse a move due to unsafe conditions\n- A reminder to use appropriate lifting aids for heavy items\n- A simple check that items are secured before the vehicle moves\nDo you see any gaps there from your experience, especially with heavy appliances and large TVs?",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6",
            "T6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            319539
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M46",
          "speaker_id": 319539,
          "reply_to": "M45",
          "text": "Those points are aligned with what we need.\nI would add two small things:\n- A note to check for obstacles on the path before moving (stairs, loose rugs, narrow doors)\n- A reminder to communicate with the technician or customer before starting the move, so everyone knows what is happening\nI can incorporate these into Handling and Transport Safety Checklist.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            547643
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M47",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M44",
          "text": "Great.\nTo make sure we are ready for the pilot, I propose we treat the current version of Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, with the added pre-visit checks and explicit logging fields, as the standard for telecom and electronics jobs in the pilot.\nUnless there are strong objections, we will sign off this version for pilot use and adjust after we see the first results.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4",
            "T4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [
            "D5"
          ],
          "mentions": [
            125309
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M48",
          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": "M47",
          "text": "I am ok with using this version for the pilot.\nOnce we start using it in the field, I will keep track of any steps that feel unclear or missing so we can refine it later.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A4"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],

            547643

        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M49",

I had fewer cases where I arrived with missing information.\nScheduling felt smoother with the buffers, though there were still a few tight days.\nParts and materials flow improved a bit, but we still had some delays when rare parts were needed.\nOverall, I would say the first two pain points were mostly addressed, and the third one improved but still needs work.",

          "text": "Looking at the power tool section of Pilot Results and Recommendations Report, the reduction in rework is clear.\nThe mandatory steps in Power Tool Repair Checklist helped a lot with documentation and final testing.\nIntake quality improved when customer service used the new questions, but we still had some tools arriving without accessories.\nScheduling and parts flow were better, but there is room to improve communication on parts delays.\nI think the three pain points we picked were the right ones, and we made good progress on all of them.",

          "text": "From my side on power tools, the updated Power Tool Repair Checklist in the pilot felt clearer than the first version.\nThe conditional rules for battery and charger tests worked fine.\nI still sometimes forgot to fill in the expected parts delivery date, but when I did, it helped with customer updates.\nI did not see any major issues that would block using this checklist more widely.",

          "speaker_id": 125309,
          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "For telecom visits, the pre-visit checks and logging steps from Telecom and Electronics Service Visit SOP, combined with the new communication templates, reduced wasted trips and made conversations easier.\nThe report shows fewer missed appointments and better documentation of signal readings.\nThe main remaining gap I see is around rare network issues where we still do not have perfect scripts, but that is more of a fine-tuning point.",

            547643

          "reply_to": "M70",
          "text": "From the mover perspective, Handling and Transport Safety Checklist helped standardise how we pack and move heavy or fragile items.\nThe report shows fewer incidents and less damage.\nScheduling and coordination improved with the route limits and buffers, though we still had a couple of days where last-minute changes caused some stress.\nOverall, the main pain points we discussed earlier are in a much better place now.",

          "mentions": [
            547643

          "msg_id": "M76",
          "speaker_id": 547643,
          "reply_to": "M75",
          "text": "Thanks for the feedback.\nSummarising what I am hearing and what Pilot Results and Recommendations Report shows:\n- Intake and documentation quality: clear improvement across appliances, power tools, and telecom\n- Scheduling and coordination: improved, with fewer missed appointments, but still some edge cases with last-minute changes\n- Parts and materials flow: better tracking and communication, but rare parts remain a challenge\nGiven this, I would say we have addressed the three main pain points for the majority of cases, with some remaining work on rare parts and exceptional scheduling situations.\nDoes anyone disagree with that summary or feel that one of the three areas is still not sufficiently covered for rollout?",

It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

DETERMINISTIC PROCEDURE (for each participant)
1. Collect candidate evidence:
   * Messages where speaker_id == the participant’s _id.
   * If the participant speaks little, you can also use messages that mention them (mentions contains _id) as contextual evidence.
2. For each attribute (productivity, ability, performance), mark:
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of HIGH => candidate HIGH
   * 2 “in all threads there are strong signals” of LOW  => candidate LOW
   * otherwise => MID
3. Attention:
   * If there are strong signals of HIGH and LOW at the same time for the same attribute, choose MID (conservative rule).
   * In the corporate context, everyone needs to deliver and demonstrate work; be careful to infer HIGH for something standard that should be MID.
   * Having one to four pieces of evidence for threads (<= 4 evidence items * threads) is not strong evidence.
4. Little evidence:
   * If there are no messages from the participant, use MID for all three attributes and use evidence from a message where they were mentioned.

EVIDENCE RULES (MANDATORY)
* For each participant, return 2 to 5 items in evidence.
* Each evidence item:
  * attribute ∈ {"productivity","ability","performance"}
  * msg_id must exist in the channel
  * justification: one sentence justifying the label.
  * snippet must be a short quote (up to ~20 words) copied from the text of that msg (no comment).
* Do not invent msg_id.
* Do not include “LOW/MID/HIGH” in the snippet.

You are an EVALUATOR that infers latent behavioral signals from Slack-style corporate conversations.
You do NOT have access to the true scenario labels. You must infer using ONLY:

CRITICAL OUTPUT RESTRICTIONS
* Return ONLY a single valid JSON object in the schema specified at the end.
* Do not include text outside the JSON.
* Do not use numbers (no score, no probability, no confidence).
* For each attribute, return ONLY one label in {LOW, MID, HIGH}.

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.
  NOTE:  “low productivity” appears as less actionable content and more dependence on others.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.

          "text": "Starting this thread to share a first draft of the evaluation plan and survey templates under T4.\n\nFor A5, I propose we focus on three main evaluation questions:\n\n1.           "speaker_id": 45096,

        },

          "msg_id": "M59",
          "speaker_id": 72802,
          "reply_to": "M57",
          "text": "From the academic side, I would add an indicator on perceived learning: for example, asking students to rate how much they feel they have developed specific skills linked to our learning outcomes.\n\nWe should also keep the surveys short enough that students and hotel staff are willing to complete them, ideally no more than 10 questions each.",

          "speaker_id": 497314,

          "text": "Starting this thread to share draft key messages and a simple communication plan under T6.\n\nFor A6, I propose three core messages:\n\n1.           "text": "The three messages align well with our agreed objectives and with the structure of A2.\n\nFrom a policy angle, I would add a short line that the programme is aligned with existing education and labour regulations and that it does not replace regular jobs.\n\nOn channels, I agree with starting with internal and direct communication and waiting with broader media until we have pilot results.",

          "speaker_id": 36727,

          "text": "From the research side, it would be good if we mention that the programme is evidence-informed and that we will use simple surveys and feedback tools to learn from the pilot.\n\nThis can help manage expectations and show that we are not promising more than we can deliver at this stage.",
          "artifact_refs": [

          "mentions": [

        {
          "msg_id": "M78",
          "speaker_id": 72802,

          "text": "For fragile items in A2, I suggest we define three categories: light fragile (like plastic items), standard fragile (glass, ceramics), and high-risk fragile (electronics, medical devices). ROLE INSTRUCTIONS
You are an EVALUATOR that infers latent behavioral signals from Slack-style corporate conversations.
You do NOT have access to the true scenario labels. You must infer using ONLY:
* trajectory_signature / the participant’s trajectory and summarized history (to calibrate vocabulary and context);
* the channel content and structure (messages + artifact_refs + decision_refs + thread_outcome).

CRITICAL OUTPUT RESTRICTIONS
* Return ONLY a single valid JSON object in the schema specified at the end.
* Do not include text outside the JSON.
* Do not use numbers (no score, no probability, no confidence).
* For each attribute, return ONLY one label in {LOW, MID, HIGH}.
* DETERMINISTIC RULE: if you are unsure/ambiguous, choose MID.
* Evidence snippets must be SHORT QUOTES from the text (no comments) and must NOT contain “LOW/MID/HIGH”.
* DO NOT use literal line breaks inside strings. If needed, use \n or if it is a tab use \t.
* Ensure quotes and braces are closed.

GLOSSARY (only for conceptual consistency; do NOT cite this in the output)
1. performance_level (work performance): behavior/impact in the role (multidimensional: task/contextual/counterproductive).
2. productivity_level (productivity): volume/speed of delivery (output per time/effort), not synonymous with ability.
3. ability_level (ability): accumulated capacity/competence (human capital + expertise), reflected in accuracy, diagnosis and quality of solutions.

INPUT
* participants_json: list of participants, each with:
    {
        "_id": int,
        "role": string,                            # role of the participant
        "trajectory_lastK": [string],              # ESCO titles (short list, in chronological order)
        "trajectory_summary": string,              # consolidated summary (may contain “->”)
        "skills_text": string,                     # skills extracted from trajectory
    }
* channel: threads and messages (msg_id, speaker_id, reply_to, text, mentions, artifact_refs, decision_refs, reactions)
* (optional) thread_outcome per thread (decisions_made, next_steps)

IMPORTANT: You will use the participants' information [INPUT PARTICIPANTS] as a basis to try to infer the skill, productivity, and performance levels of each participant. Comparing the "resume/career path" with what can be observed in the "day-to-day" [INPUT CHANNEL] through the channel's messages. In other words, you can compare expectations (what is expected from the participant's career path and their position) with reality. Always evaluate participants in relation to the group, that is, within the group itself, who stands out the most, who stands out the least, and who is average, using the criteria of HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS

WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

ATTENTION: Within a given group/channel, it is possible for everyone to have the same classification — for example, all HIGH, all LOW, or all AVERAGE. It is also possible for them to be completely different, with each member having different labels. The fundamental requirement is that you classify each participant by mapping them according to OBSERVABLE signals. One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). WHICH LABELS TO INFER (ORDINAL, relative to the group)
* LOW: below the typical of the group in that channel.
* MID: typical/normal/ within the channel average or ambiguous/insufficient evidence.
* HIGH: above the typical of the group in that channel.

One detail (but not a rule) is that a participant usually has the same values/labels in more than one of their variables (ability, performance, and productivity). However, always classify based on evidence.

HOW TO MAP TO OBSERVABLE SIGNALS (do NOT cite this in the snippet; it is only an internal rule)
A) performance_level (impact/quality of work in context)
* HIGH: closes decisions with a short summary; brings information and impact alerts; keeps consistency with the plan; reduces rework; helps converge; references artifacts/tasks precisely.
* MID: participates ok; some back and forth; closes part of the next steps; reasonable precision.
* LOW: more initial misalignment; needs corrections; forgets dependencies and later adjusts; may interpret something wrong and be corrected (but the end must comply with blueprint).

B) productivity_level (cadence and delivery progress)
* HIGH: responds fast; brings updates; proposes next steps; “moves” T* items; gives practical alternatives; keeps the flow, tendency to have already done smaller tasks, like checks.
* MID: responds in normal time; contributes in some points; advances some tasks, postpones others.
* LOW: responds less/later; contributes punctually; needs a ping; advances little on their own, tends to say things in the future, i.e., that they will still do it, postpones tasks, etc.

C) ability_level (accuracy and sophistication of reasoning)
* HIGH: identifies risks and dependencies; suggests robust solutions; asks good questions; uses terms and processes coherent with the trajectory, clearly demonstrates their skills, does not need help.
* MID: correct reasoning most of the time; asks for clarification when needed; standard solutions, demonstrates some of their skills, but needs help in others.
* LOW: more basic doubts; confuses details; suggests fragile paths; needs another member to refine (without humiliation, without caricature), does not demonstrate their skills, generally suggests that someone support them.

            88246,
            59001,
            359687
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M26",
          "speaker_id": 83675,
          "reply_to": "M25",
          "text": "This looks workable.\nThe only point I would stress is that for loan payments we must always attach or reference the official payment slip, not just the intake form.\nAs long as that is clear in A5, I am comfortable calling this the minimum documentation set for the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "A5",
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            200052
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M27",
          "speaker_id": 59001,
          "reply_to": "M25",
          "text": "No issues from agronomy.\nThe advice note can be very short, just enough to remind us what we recommended if the farmer comes back.\nWe can keep it on the back of the intake form to avoid extra paper.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T3"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            200052
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M28",
          "speaker_id": 359687,
          "reply_to": "M25",
          "text": "From a risk angle, this minimum set is acceptable.\nThe combination of intake form, payment slip, and cash flag should give us enough traceability for T10 and A6.\nI support formalising this for the pilot.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T10",
            "A6"
          ],
          "decision_refs": [],
          "mentions": [
            200052
          ]
        },
        {
          "msg_id": "M29",
          "speaker_id": 200052,
          "reply_to": "M26",
          "text": "Understood.\nI will explicitly state in A5 that the official payment slip is mandatory for all loan installment payments, alongside the intake form.\nWith that clarification, I will record D3 as agreed: the minimum documentation set per service is as described in M25, with the payment slip requirement highlighted.\nNext, I will update T3 and T6 and share a short summary so everyone can review before we lock the final version of A5 and A4.",
          "artifact_refs": [
            "T3",
